The Ilm comes up over the Fishstairs, stands on the second step at the Cross on Account-day, and goes around both the clean dark line at the Vail corner and the burned line two doors down; she stands over the standing line and the new finer grey with a broom and sweeps neither, and gives the broom its instruction before anybody. No opening comes in seven days and the widow’s mark is not touched once. On Silt 13 she carries him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and no slate opened, and asks nothing about the sixth page or the tin; the arrangement with Alda holds without a word. She does not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stays cold, though it is told of her that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everyone was kind, and the boy does not lay the two together. At dusk of the last day she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, and leaves the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the flood, the cold foot, the two lines and the empty place beside the one crust, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 75 through 77 the keeping takes the measure of a recovery that is another kind of avoidance. The yard sweeps around what the water left and calls the new grey thaw, and she stands over both lines with a broom and sweeps neither; a figure goes from fist to mouth to shoulder and arrives nowhere, and she answers a woman who wants it by sending her to the pot. A warm loaf passes from a man from Slate Row into a foundling’s pocket with no slate between them, and she neither looks nor connects the two. The half-pace, the unentered basket, the untouched mark and the private roll all hold exactly as they held before the flood; the wall has acquired no door, and the boy is still not written as Vail.

On Days 78 through 84 the keeping takes the measure of a lean week that changes nothing and adds no explanation. The flood has gone into mud that sets into a brown skin over the ruts, and she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody: go around what the water left, the clean dark line at the Vail corner, the new finer grey beside it and the space under the lowest rack, because it cost enough to come in and will cost more to take out. She sweeps none of them. The house keeps its number in loaves moved along a shelf, glances at the clay jar and a space at the row’s end nobody calls a figure, while she says \emph{the house}, sends every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom, and never to the basket. Three doors down she sets the basket at the edge of the light away from any open slate and stands a half-pace from Alda’s writing; at the well she goes wide around a slate set out to dry and does not touch the mark. When a second man come downriver from Greybank tells the bucket-round of a counting room shut in the war with the men inside dead of the breath, she tells the fire it is the thaw and lets it lie, joining nothing to her roof. No opening comes in seven days and the mark hangs where it hangs. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the gone board, the cold foot and the empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 85 through 90 the keeping takes the measure of a month turning on the same mud it came in on, and adds no explanation. The boy is eighty-five through ninety days old, three months at the close, and she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. On Silt 26 and Seed 1 she gives the broom its instruction before she gives it to anybody --- go around what the water left, it cost enough to come in, it will cost more to take out --- stands over the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, and sweeps none of them; when a woman asks what the month will cost she moves her lips along the loaf shelf, glances at the clay jar and tells her to ask the pot. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; she says the house where another woman would say I. When the second telling of the shut counting room goes over the bucket she tells the fire it is the thaw and joins nothing to her roof, though she lost a husband to that danger and has never once described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, stands a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show, and asks nothing. On Silt 30 she sets him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr reads one in twelve over fewer bodies and takes himself out of his own sentence, and carries him home saying nothing about what was read over him. No opening came in six days and a month’s turning is not an opening, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is. At the turn into Seed the first work is sweeping and the work after it lies east of Low Kiln in strips she has not gone to see. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the second telling, the thinner crowd, the out-of-line landing, the foundling’s half-beat, the turned slate, the cold foot and the unnamed empty place, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 91–93 the keeping takes the measure of the first planting week and adds no explanation. The house’s work moves east of Low Kiln into strips she goes around with a broom and a look, and her rule holds exactly: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the strips, House Silt and the Fishstairs. On Seed 2 she gives the broom its instruction before anybody, goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeps none of them, and at the well sends a woman asking the planting cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}, leaving the empty place at the row’s end with no figure. She tells the fire it is the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot; its payer has gone unnamed for ninety-three days. No opening came in three days --- not a strip, a broom, a basket, a well, a market, a door or a bed --- so the widow’s mark hung where it hangs; she has lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she sets the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opens none and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, standing a half-pace off while Alda presses the fold too long and writes what she will not show. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Mira’s cords, Berr’s box and Alda’s tin all stay as they were. At dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; the private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door.

Through Days 94 through 100 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become waiting and adds no explanation. The house’s arithmetic is now two empty places on the loaf shelf --- the old space at the row’s end nobody calls a number and a new gap that came in the night of Seed 5 --- and she moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar, gives the instruction to the pot, the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, and says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. To a woman at the well she says ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there, because \emph{the house has said it}, and leaves the space at the row’s end with no figure. She goes around the brown skin holding a boot-print, the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack with a broom and a glance and sweeps none of them, telling the fire it is the thaw each day and turning the coals with the back of a broken pot. The carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred days and the coal the gull took is entered in no slate. No opening came in seven days --- a strip, a shelf, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark stayed where it hung; she lost a husband to that danger and has never described it that way herself. Three doors down she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, opened none and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the going of the light on Day 100 she set the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped; the river’s note came through the finger’s-width-open door and the fire’s four, four and a gap through the floor, in two separate places as for a hundred days. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and nothing was joined, paid, explained or ended. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

Through Days 101 through 103 the keeping takes the measure of a planting month that has become three ordinary days of two absences nobody joins. A neighbour at the loaf shelf reaches past the bare board, names the row’s old space as a thing the planting brought in and the empty place at the boy’s ear as a child’s appetite in one breath, takes her loaf and goes with her pot; Sella moves her lips along the row, glances at the clay jar and leaves both gaps with no figure, and does not hear the two places as one. On Seed 13 she agrees with the early thaw and the late and keeps wanting the late because it puts off the paying; Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and the household straightens around his silence, and a neighbour at the bucket-round only mentions a room shut in the war with men dead of the breath, which she answers by telling the fire it is the thaw and joining nothing to her roof. On Seed 14 she sets the basket at the end of the fish-trade shade where no slate lies and then three doors down just inside a finger’s-width-open door, opens no slate and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. Every instruction goes to the fire, the wool, the water, the pot and the broom and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, tells the fire the thaw each day and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot. No opening came in three days, so the widow’s mark hung where it hung; the carried fire’s payer has gone unnamed for a hundred and three days and the two lines in the corner stayed unswept. At dusk each day she set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen, carrying one crust and its unnamed empty place and two shelf gaps in another room that does not touch it. The private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the wall has acquired no door.

On Days 104 through 106 the keeping takes the measure of the hands going into the strips and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and four, then one hundred and five, then one hundred and six days old and nobody under the roof says so. She gives the instruction to the broom and the bucket before anybody and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the well, the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, and goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. At the loaf shelf she hears a neighbour name the old gap and the boy’s empty place in one breath and leaves both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence; the T097 witness is advanced, not paid. She hears the yard want the thaw early and late, agrees with both and wants the late because it puts off the paying. Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence and Tarn’s knife and seventh year go unremarked: the household still straightens around a silence the way cloth straightens when a weight is lifted. She tells the fire it is the thaw through all three days and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and six days; the fire keeps its four low pulls and the missing fifth, and the carried fire stays under blind ash and the back of a broken pot. No opening comes in three days --- a strip, a shelf, a rack, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings --- so the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs. Each dusk she sets the boy on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joining, the near-spoken number of hands, the men in the back room, the seventh year at the edge of the sill and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 107 through 109 the keeping takes the measure of the planting month entering its last tend and an Account-day read over the worked strips, and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and seven, then one hundred and eight, then one hundred and nine days old and nobody under the roof says so. Every instruction goes to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the wheel-shed, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, the Cross, the moot-post’s shade and three doors down, and goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. At the loaf shelf she hears a neighbour name the row’s old gap as a thing the planting brought in and go off with her pot without seeing the empty place at his ear, and hears a second say it two days later; she leaves both gaps unfigured, hearing two sayings and not one absence, and the T097 witness advances toward the far-off finger without being paid. She gives the instruction to the broom before she gives it to anybody, and Tarn takes it only then and sweeps the collector’s road without turning along it while his seventh year lies at the very edge of the sill and his breath stays unspent. On Seed 19 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gives the end of it to the pot and the household straightens around his silence, and she gives the house no name for the men. She tells the fire it is the thaw on all three days and turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; at the fire she counts something under her breath and pushes a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, and the grey streak at her temple shows pale. No opening comes in three days — a strip, a shelf, a rack, a wheel-shed, a market, a reading, a door and a bed are not openings — so the widow’s mark hangs where it hangs and the private roll stays unshown. Each dusk she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face and leaves the thread frozen; one brown-edged crust lies stiff in the fold with its empty place unnamed and the shelf keeps two gaps in a room that does not touch it. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joinings, the men in the back room, the seventh year at the edge of the sill and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch.

On Days 110 through 112 the keeping takes the measure of the planting month’s last tend and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and never in the Debt Loft. Every instruction goes to the bucket, the broom, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house}, moves her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glances at the clay jar and gives nobody a figure, and leaves a neighbour’s one-breath joining unjoined and the widow’s mark untouched, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a well, a market, a post, a road, a door, a basket and a bed are not openings. At the well she sends a woman asking the planting’s cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}; at the fire she tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot and feeds them, says \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and stands a moment counting under her breath toward no opening with the grey streak pale at her temple, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist and not looking toward the bed. On Seed 22 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, the household straightening around his silence; the debt’s broom checks half a beat behind the wheel-keeper’s finger and goes on, and she asks nothing about either. Three doors down she stands a half-pace off while Alda writes what she will not show and asks nothing about the writing, the tin or the date over a dead woman’s sign. No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown, she has not written him as Vail, and the wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the third shaping of the shelf’s absence, the first small change in the two silences under the roof, the fist that would not give its number and the two empty places in rooms that do not touch, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Days 113 through 115 the keeping takes the measure of the planting’s last tend and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the loaf shelf, the worked strips, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs, the Cross and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at the going of the light and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped. Every instruction goes to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house}, moves her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glances at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gives nobody a figure, and sends a woman with wet sleeves to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}. She hears a neighbour lay the shelf’s old space and the empty place at his ear under one cause in a single breath and does not make the joining either, and the witness advances unpaid. At the fire she tells it the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, feeds them and says \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting under her breath toward no opening, her grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed. On Seed 25 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; the household straightens around his silence and the debt’s broom goes on over the flagstones without the check it made the day before, the stones keeping the stopped place, and she asks nothing about either. No opening comes in three days, the widow’s mark hangs untouched, the private roll stays unshown, and she has not said whose child he is. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the neighbour’s one-breath joining, the fist that would not give its figure, the moved equality under the roof, the two shelf gaps and the empty place in the fold, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 116 through 119 the keeping takes the measure of the planting’s end and crosses into Reed without an entry. She carried him to the very edge of the worked strips and stood a half-pace from every open slate with the basket held level, giving the instruction to the wool and the river wind and never to the basket, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}; the last hands came out of the strips and one place in the line was gone around with a look and no figure, and she went around it as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering nothing. Back under the roof she gave the bucket, broom, pot and fire their instructions before anybody and never the basket, moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf is not an opening. At the well and in the yard she sent women asking the planting’s cost to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} On all four days she told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it}; she stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. She carried him to the wheel-shed’s edge of light, the stalls beyond the Cross, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the moot-post’s shade, setting the basket where no slate lay and opening none. With Jorra men unnamed came before first grey and his bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and asked nothing. With Tarn the exact account held and she did not ask about his seventh year or his ear. No opening came in four days, the mark hung where it hung, the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the missing hand, the neighbours’ joinings, the green at a mouth, the clerk’s uncalled measure and a count nobody will say, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

Through Reed 1–3, Y.H. 813 the keeping takes the measure of a month turning toward the reed beds and adds no explanation. She carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the worked strips’ edge, the stalls beyond the Cross, the road downriver, the Weir and under the roof, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light and putting the fold right without a look at his face, the thread left frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed. Every instruction went to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the fire, the wool and the river wind and never to the basket; she said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, sent a woman who asked what the reeds would cost to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and told a man who asked what the work would want to ask the river. She went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack and the missing hand’s place in the strip as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering none of them. At the loaf shelf she moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gave nobody a figure, and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a market and a bed are not openings. On all three days she told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed. On Reed 2 men unnamed before first grey went low-voiced into the back room and Jorra’s bent finger went into the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and asked nothing, and Tarn’s stroke went on without the half-check while the stones kept the place where it had stopped. No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is; the fire’s missing fifth breath went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-two days and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed in rooms that do not touch. The wall has acquired no door.

On Days 123 through 125 the keeping takes the measure of the reed month’s first days and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the worked strips’ edge, the Weir and the stalls beyond the Cross, and each going of the light up the clay road and under the roof, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face and leaving the thread frozen. The instruction goes to the wool, the river wind, the bucket, the broom, the pot and the fire, and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, goes wide around the space beneath the lowest rack and the empty place in the strip, and sends a woman asking the reeds’ cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}. At the loaf shelf her lips move along a row standing with two gaps and she glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gives nobody a figure; the two rooms do not touch and no neighbour names the gaps in these three days. On all three days she tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, feeds them and says \emph{The house will keep it}, standing a moment counting under her breath toward no opening and pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light. On Reed 5 men unnamed come before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger goes into the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, so the end of it arrives at the pot and the household straightens around his silence; she asks nothing. She is within hearing on Reed 5 when Tarn’s sentence comes to the threshold of the word and goes back, and asks nothing, because a question said aloud becomes a thing a house must answer. Through all three days the carried fire keeps four, four and a gap with its payer unnamed for a hundred and twenty-five days, the river’s note comes through the finger’s-width-open door, the boards keep four nails, four and a knot, and the three counts do not become one. No opening came, the widow’s mark was not touched, and she has still not said whose child he is.

On Days 126 through 128 the keeping takes the measure of the first counted bundles of Reed and adds no explanation. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the stalls beyond the Cross, the Weir, House Silt three doors down and back under the roof each going of the light, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face and leaves the thread frozen, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it goes away. At the yard the reeds stand green at the broken ends and pale at the tips; a woman who asks what they cost is sent to the pot with \emph{the house has said it}, a man who asks what the beds will want is given the weather, and the question arrives nowhere held level. She goes around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack and the place in the strip where a hand did not come back, entering none of them, and does not touch the widow’s mark at a rack, a strip, a well, a yard, a market, a road, a basket, a bed or a dusk. At the Cross she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade and keeps a half-pace from every slate; at the Weir she goes around a propped slate and sets him at the edge of the work; three doors down she stands a half-pace off while Alda writes and asks nothing about the slates, the tin or the date. At the fire she tells it the thaw on all three days, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes the coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, sets the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and does not look toward the bed. She hears Tarn’s sentence come a second time to the word that would call the loan and stop there, and asks nothing within hearing; Jorra’s dust, the unnamed men and the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence go unasked about. The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the cost asked as a direction, the second stopping, the third green, the four unread records downriver and the lie curdling three doors down, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 129 through 131 the house goes on keeping what it cannot enter, and the woman who keeps it adds one unexplained motion: a finger beneath the loaf shelf, withdrawn without a look. The charcoal under the board has been there longer than the boy’s notice of it, and her hand goes to it as her hand goes to the pot, the broom and the fire. She has still not said whose fire, whose child or whose count. The wall has acquired no door.

On Days 132 through 134 the keeping adds a second motion to the first: a finger beneath the board twice in three days, withdrawn without a look, and a count under the breath at the fire toward no opening. The charcoal under the shelf has been there longer than the boy’s notice of it and her hand goes to it as her hand goes to the pot, the broom and the fire; it stays unread and separate from the two gaps above and the crust in the fold in a room that does not touch. She has still not said whose fire, whose child or whose count, and she hears a fourth stopping without asking and a man come before first grey without naming him. The wall has acquired no door.

On Days 135 through 137 the keeping takes the measure of the reed month’s last third and adds one more unexplained motion. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the reed beds’ edge, the wheel-shed’s edge, the Weir’s plank walk, the Cross, the market stalls and back under the roof each going of the light, giving the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, and saying \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. At the loaf shelf on Day 135 she reaches a finger beneath the board where the charcoal tally lies, without looking or a word, and brings it away and does not go back; a hand that goes under without looking either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, and the reason is left between the two. She goes wide around every open slate, the two unswept lines called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates and the place in the returning line gone around with a look and no number. Men unnamed come before first grey on Day 136 and she gives the house no name for them; Jorra’s dust and his finger in the damper go unasked about, and within hearing of Tarn’s fifth stopping she ends her instruction at the pot and asks nothing, and neither man names the other’s silence. At the going of the light on Day 137 she sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without a look at his face, leaves the thread frozen, tells the fire it was the thaw, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening and sets the pot handle two inches beyond the hand that will not close on it. No opening came in three days, the mark hung where it hung, the private roll stayed unshown and the wall acquired no door.

On Days 138 through 140 the keeping takes the measure of the reed month’s last tend and adds nothing to what it will explain. She carries him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard and the edge of the worked strips, the loaf shelf and hearth, the Cross and the stalls, the out-of-line landing, the Weir’s plank walk and blessing stone, the fish-trade shade, and up the clay road each going of the light, giving the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, and saying \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}. The shelf keeps its two unnamed gaps and the charcoal under the board stays on a place of its own; on Days 138 and 140 her finger goes beneath the front edge without a look or a word and comes away, and a hand that goes under without looking either knows the board by heart or has been told not to look, the reason left between the two. She goes wide around the two lines called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, entering none. Men unnamed come before first grey on Day 140 and she gives the house no name for them and does not say the room was cold; within hearing of the sixth stopping she ends her instruction at the pot and asks nothing, and neither man names the other’s silence. At the fire on all three days she tells it it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the hand that will not close on it and does not look toward the bed, the payer unnamed for one hundred and thirty-eight, one hundred and thirty-nine and one hundred and forty days. No opening came in three days, the mark hung where it hung, the private roll stayed unshown and the wall acquired no door.

Through Reed 22–24 the keeping goes on at the same half-pace and the same wall stays unbreached. He gives every instruction to the wool, the wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, answers cost with the weather, the river, the pot and the house, and carries him up from the Weir, down from the Cross and around the rack space and the empty place with a look and a wide step. Twice more a finger goes beneath the loaf shelf where the charcoal tally lies — once on Day 141 and twice on Day 143 — without a look or a word, and the reason stands between knowing the board by heart and having been told not to look. She gives no name to the men who go low into the back room on Day 142, does not say the room was cold and asks nothing about Tarn’s seventh stopping, heard from within earshot; the equality under the roof is none of her business to speak of. The boy is set on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft, the fold put right without a look at his face, the thread left frozen, the pot handle two inches beyond his reaching hand, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it goes away. The grey streak shows pale off the coals; the widow’s mark stays untouched because a shelf, an afternoon, a yard, a bed and a dusk are not openings. Nothing has been explained and no bond has changed hands.

Through Reed 25–27 the reed month goes out without a boundary and the keeping goes on at the same half-pace with the same wall unbreached. On Day 144 she carried him to the Clay Yard among the last bundles, judged by the arm that carried them rather than by a figure, and went around the clean dark line, the newer hairline called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates and the empty place in the returning line with a look and a wide step and no number. A girl with a creel was told her arm knew what went into a bundle and that was the whole of it; a man who asked what the hands would be paid was answered with the weather and the river and carried no figure away. At the shelf she set the basket low where the underside of the board becomes a roof and reached a finger BENEATH it without looking; the marks stayed unread and separate from the two gaps above and the crust in the other room. She told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, and set the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand. On Day 145 men unnamed came low into the back room before first grey and she carried past at the half-pace, turned no head, gave them no name and did not say the room was cold; Jorra’s dust and the damper ahead of her sentence went unasked about, and within hearing of the eighth stopping she ended her instruction at the pot and asked nothing, neither man naming the other’s silence. On Day 146 she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down at the edge of the light, away from every open slate, and stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote, asking nothing; at dusk she went around a pan set out to dry and the trough by the well with its skin of ice, set him on his bed, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread of drool frozen and unwiped, and went to her own bed without explaining the count. No opening came in three days, the widow’s mark was not touched and the private roll stayed unshown. Nothing was explained and no bond changed hands.

On Days 147 through 149 the reed month goes out and the taking stays a taking done as maintenance: the half-pace from every open slate, the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, \emph{The house will keep it} said to the fire, and the widow’s mark hanging where it hangs because a shelf, an afternoon, a strip, a market, a bed and a dusk are not openings. On Day 147 her finger goes beneath the loaf shelf where the charcoal tally lies, without looking or a word, and comes away; on Day 148 she gives the men who go low into the back room no name and within hearing of Tarn’s ninth stopping gives the end of her instruction to the pot and asks nothing; on Day 149 she sets the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade while the last market sells over the clerk and nothing in the square is joined. Each dusk she carries him up the clay road around the pan and the iced trough, sets him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, leaves the thread frozen, rests her hand a half-beat longer than the setting and goes to her own bed without explaining the count. The private roll stays unshown, her silence about the payer of any warmth stays a wall, and the two rooms do not touch.

\textbf{Ch 37.} For a hundred and forty-nine days she had gone around every opening because none was an opening; on Day 150, the first firing of Tallow, she put her hand to the widow’s mark before the kiln mouth, held it one breath, let go, tipped the carried coal under the back of a broken pot and went back to setting pots, and did not touch the mark again at a shelf, a well, an afternoon or a dusk. The fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and fifty, then a hundred and fifty-one, then a hundred and fifty-two days. She gave the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot and the broom and never to the basket, carried him at the half-pace from every open slate, went around the pan’s gone place, the trough now without its skin of ice and wide around the rack space, told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, counted under her breath toward no opening and set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand. At the Weir on Day 151 she answered a woman who asked what the hands would be paid with the going down and the coming back and then the river, and sent a neighbour with a wet pot at the kiln-house to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}. Standing with her back to the basket on that afternoon she moved her lips along the row with its two gaps and reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread). On Day 152, within hearing of Tarn’s stopped sentence, she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; she did not ask Jorra about his dust or the damper and he did not ask about the ear. She carried him up each dusk and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, and went to her own bed without explaining the count. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no name for the payer.

\textbf{Ch 38.} Through Tallow 4–10 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace from every open slate, and the widow’s mark hanging where it hung at every shelf, well, afternoon and dusk, because none was an opening. On Day 154 three or four men went low into the finger’s-width-open back room before first grey; she carried past at the half-pace, turned no head, gave the house no name for them and did not say the room was cold, and Jorra’s dusty finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence while she told the fire it was low. On Day 155 at the Weir she set the basket at the edge of the work where no slate lay and answered a woman who asked what the hands were paid with the going down and the coming back and then the river. On Day 156, when a woman raking the kiln mouth spoke sideways of a man in Mud End taken in his sleep and called merciful, she told the fire it was the thaw and did not make a lesson of it; at the going of the light she set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen, let her hand rest a half-beat longer than the setting, set the pot handle two inches beyond his reach and went to her own bed, the two rooms not touching. On Day 157 a neighbour with wet sleeves asked what a firing cost set down there and was sent to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, carrying the question away level; standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row, she reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back to the shelf. At the hearth on all seven days she told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, and set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand. On Day 158 a slate-runner came through with a narrow slate held edge-on; she carried past at the half-pace and gave the house no name for it. On Day 159 she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, kept the half-pace from every open slate, and carried him home at the going of the light saying nothing about what had been read over him. The fire’s payer stayed unnamed for a hundred and fifty-nine days. No bond changed hands, no secret entered, no new scar or possession.

\textbf{Ch 39.} Through Tallow 11–13 she kept the house the way she kept the fire: instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace from every open slate, and the widow’s mark where it hung at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, bed and dusk, because none was an opening. She fed the fire under the back of a broken pot and it answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and sixty, a hundred and sixty-one and a hundred and sixty-two days; at the going of each light she told it the thaw, turned the coals, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and did not look toward the bed. She went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the bare dark trough, the pan’s gone place and the empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15, with a look and a wide step and no number. On Day 160, standing with her back to the basket, she reached a finger beneath the loaf shelf’s front edge where the charcoal lies, without looking and without a word; on Day 161 she did not go back to the shelf and did not look. To the neighbour with the wet pot she gave the cost to the pot with no figure. On Day 161 she began \emph{The fire’s low. It wants---}, and for the first time under the roof Jorra’s bent finger waited on the cold iron until she had finished \emph{It wants feeding}; she gave the end of her instruction to the pot, the household straightened around the finished sentence, and nobody said a word of the waiting. On Day 162 she carried him downriver and back at the half-pace with the basket at the edge of the work where no slate lay, and at the going of the light carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her and river wind behind, going wide around the pan’s gone place, the trough and the rack space, and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft. With Jorra she asked nothing about the men or the dust or the fraction; within hearing of Tarn’s ear-sentence at his teeth she asked nothing about his seventh year or his loan. No bond changed hands and the private roll stayed unshown.

Through Days 163–169 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace from every open slate and a going-wide around the bare trough, the pan’s gone place and the rack space with the broken birth-slates. The kiln is brought up for the third working week; the fire answers four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and sixty-three through a hundred and sixty-nine days. On Day 166, standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row, she reaches a finger beneath the front edge where the charcoal tally lies and holds it there for the length of one of the breaths she counts before bringing it away, without looking, reading or a word, and does not go back to the shelf that night. At the going of each light she sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and leaves the mark untouched. The hand rests a half-beat longer than the setting needs. Her private roll stays unshown.

\textbf{Ch 41.} Through Tallow 21–23 she keeps the house the way she keeps the fire: instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, a half-pace from every open slate, and the widow’s mark where it hung at a morning, a shelf and a dusk, because none was an opening. The kilns are brought up for the last working week and the danger gathers in the dust ground small as meal, the sweetish lead edge on a wrong wind and a pot singing before its time; she gives costs to pots, weather and rivers and no figure to anybody, and no pot is lost. On Day 171 three or four men go low into the finger’s-width-open back room before first grey and she carries past at the half-pace, turns no head, gives the house no name for them and does not say the room is cold; when her instruction goes low Jorra’s bent finger waits in the cold damper until she has finished, and the household straightens around the finished sentence with nobody speaking of the waiting. In that same breath Tarn’s broom checks half a beat behind the standing finger on the flagstones and goes on without a word or a turn of the head; she asks nothing, and the two silences stay unjoined. On all three days she tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, goes wide around the pan’s gone place, the bare dark trough and the rack space with its broken birth-slates, and carries him home up the clay road at the going of the light with woodsmoke before her and the river wind behind. Her eye goes once each day to the clay jar cold under its glaze and her hand shuts half over nothing without touching it; her finger does not go beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal waits unread. The crust stays stiff and leathery two inches from his ear with its empty place unnamed, the two rooms do not touch, and the private roll stays unshown. Nothing was joined, paid, named or ended.

Through Days 173–179 the keeping takes the measure of the firing month’s last tend and its third Account-day and adds no explanation. The kilns stand at their last heat; the fire under the broken pot keeps four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and seventy-three through a hundred and seventy-nine days. She gives every instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket, says the house, keeps her half-pace and goes wide around the clean dark line, the thaw, the rack space and the empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15. Men go low into the back room on Days 174, 176 and 178 and she gives them no name; on 174 and 178 her unfinished sentence finishes at the damper while Jorra’s finger waits, and she asks nothing. On Day 179 she sets the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off, gives the basket no instruction and no reason, and comes back at the going of the light to lift it base first and level. The widow’s mark hangs where it hangs at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, market, post and dusk, because no hour among these seven was an opening; the private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is.

Through Days 180–182 (Ember 1–3) the keeping takes the measure of a month that turns without a boundary and of an opening performed before the kiln, and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and eighty, then one hundred and eighty-one, then one hundred and eighty-two days old and nobody says so; the district keeps calling Tallow the firing month and Ember the kiln month and neither usage is corrected. She gives every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom and running water and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, goes wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the bare dark trough whose water is called weather, the pan’s gone place and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15, with a look and a wide step and no number or explanation of the turns to the basket. The fire under the broken pot keeps four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty, a hundred and eighty-one and a hundred and eighty-two days. \textbf{Her change in the chapter:} on the morning of Day 180 she touched the widow’s mark before the first firing of Ember, held it one breath, let it go, lifted the lid and tipped the carried coal under a broken pot; the fire took, nobody praised it and nobody saw what it mended, and she did not touch the mark again at any other hour of the three days because a shelf, a well, a rack, a road, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk are not openings. To a neighbour asking a cost on Day 181 she gave the pot and the weather with no figure, nothing slopped and nothing refused. On the same morning, when her instruction went low and unfinished, Jorra’s bent finger waited in the cold damper until the sentence reached the pot and the fraction stayed held and unspoken, beside the Day 166 beat and the Day 171 flagstone half-check but not paired with either. Men unnamed went into the back room before first grey on the last two mornings and she gave them no name and did not say the room was cold. She told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand and let her hand rest a half-beat longer at the setting. Her finger did not go beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal stayed unread. At each going of the light she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her and river wind behind, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread unwiped and went to her own bed; the two rooms did not touch. The private roll stayed unshown and she has not said whose child he is.

Through Days 183–185 (Ember 4–6) the keeping takes the measure of a week that settles into the kiln month’s ordinary arithmetic and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and eighty-three, then one hundred and eighty-four, then one hundred and eighty-five days old and nobody says so. She gives every instruction to the wool, fire, pot, broom and running water and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it, goes wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the bare dark trough whose water is called weather, the pan’s gone place and the empty place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15, with a look and a wide step and no number or explanation of the turns to the basket. The fire under the broken pot answers four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-three, four and five days; the carried fire keeps its one opening behind the household, the mark touched once before the kiln on Ember 1 and at no shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon or dusk since, because a morning and a shelf are not openings and the hand goes to the mark before the kiln and at no other hour. On Day 184 she sends a neighbour with a wet pot to the pot and the weather with no figure, the question carried away level with nothing slopped. On Days 184 and 185, when her instruction goes low and unfinished at the hearth, Jorra’s bent finger stands in the cold damper until the sentence reaches the pot; the fraction is held and unspoken, a remembered holding and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 beat beneath the shelf or the Day 171 flagstone half-check. Men unnamed go low into the back room before first grey on the last two mornings and she gives them no name and does not say the room is cold, and no third telling comes. She tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, counts under her breath toward no opening, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and does not look toward the bed. Her finger does not go beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal stays unread. At each going of the light she carries him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her and river wind behind, sets him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, puts the fold right without looking at his face, leaves the thread unwiped and goes to her own bed; the two rooms do not touch. She has said nothing about the stone in the loft, whose taking above her house she cannot have heard as anything but the scrape of a pot’s foot. The private roll stays unshown and she has not said whose child he is.

Through Days 186–188 (Ember 7–9) the keeping takes the measure of three ordinary days in the middle of the kiln month and adds no explanation. The boy is one hundred and eighty-six, then one hundred and eighty-seven, then one hundred and eighty-eight days old and nobody says so; the widow’s mark hangs where it hung, untouched at a morning, a shelf, a well, a rack, a basket, an afternoon and a dusk, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour. Every instruction goes to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; she says \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, keeps her half-pace from every open slate, glances once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and shuts her hand half over nothing without touching it, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, tells the fire it was the thaw, turns the coals with the back of a broken pot, says \emph{The house will keep it}, pushes coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak shows pale, counts under her breath toward no opening, and does not look toward the bed. The fire answers four low pulls with the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-six, seven and eight days, and she goes around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the bare dark trough, the pan’s gone place and the field’s empty place with a look and a wide step and no number (T088, T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). On Day 187 a neighbour come up from the tubs with a wet pot asked what the firing cost now the kiln month’s middle days were on; she glanced once at the clay jar, shut her hand half over nothing and sent the question to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried it away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, paid small and non-fatally:} on Day 188, after a rack-worker’s pot gave its note before its time and sang itself out early with the woman going on with her hands and making no lesson of it, two men carried a glaze-room hand out of the kiln and across the yard toward the clay road, one with a thumb hooked under his arm to keep the head from lopping. She set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned the boy’s face as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it, went wide around the place the carriers crossed, and gave the yard no name for what ailed him; nobody called a collector, gave a figure or opened a slate, and the cost stayed entered nowhere (T077 advanced, not paid). At the going of the light each day she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before her in long low bars and river wind behind, and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled as a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, the thread left frozen and unwiped. Her finger did not go beneath the front edge of the loaf shelf on any of the three days; the charcoal tally stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100 carried). Her end of the instruction waited at the hearth on all three days while Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper and the sentence reached the pot, the fraction a remembered holding and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 shelf beat or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T062). The wall has acquired no door: it keeps out the pale line at the gum, the sweet breath on the wrong wind, the cost carried up the road unentered, the two men’s passage across the yard and the number nobody says, and keeps the boy warm without ever entering the warmth.

On Days 189 through 191 she carries him at the half-pace from every open slate, gives the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket, says \emph{the house}, sets the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand, and leaves the widow’s mark where it hangs, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1. On the first Account-day of Ember she sets the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lies and stands half a pace off through the reading and the bell, giving no reason to the basket; on the two mornings after she sends women’s cost-questions to the pot and the weather and goes wide around the unswept places and the place the carriers crossed with a look and a wide step and no number. Her finger stays from beneath the loaf shelf and the charcoal stays unread. The fire’s payer goes unnamed for a hundred and eighty-nine, ninety and ninety-one days, and the cost of the man carried out on Day 188 is entered nowhere.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Did not enter the birth room and said nothing. Woodsmoke and wet wool came ahead of her, then the cold off the yard, then the hand with the little-door burn across its back --- lintel, threshold, two straight sides. It felt for heat at the child’s belly, found none, opened and shut once above the covered bundle and withdrew. She stepped back out into the Clay Yard without looking at child or women. The crust and the warmed stone had already come from her hearth, neither entered against anybody; the kiln breathed through the wall afterward. She still intends to take him on the third day.

\item Ch 2: Kept the fire and the house through Days 2 and 3. At first light touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, gave instruction to the pot and the fire, would not let anyone fill Garl’s seat or take his coat down, and said the house kept a roll of its own. Announced that the boy would come under the roof and was answered \emph{he’s not Vail}; got quieter and did not reply. On the third morning came for him, crossed to the bench first, lifted him with the little-door hand, said \emph{the boy} and \emph{the house}, carried him up the Clay Yard and laid him on fresh straw. Gave the bed to the foundling and the loft to Tarn without explaining either, told the pot it would pay for itself in the thaw, and left the charred slate in the kiln ash untouched.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Carried the boy out of the kiln-house in a basket under a fold of wool --- he left the house and its heat went out behind him --- and held him like a pot filled that must not be slopped. Did not touch the widow’s mark, since the coals were only being banked. Counted off the question of the mother with \emph{Account-day} and the question of the house with \emph{the house}; put the fold back over his face and ears without looking and spoke the instruction to the wool and the wind. Kept a half-pace from the slate on the block and did not set the basket where it lay open. At the Slate Row end refused to answer Berr about the confirmed widow’s mark, pulled the wool over the boy’s ear, and let the uncalled debt lie. Lifted the basket off the post in the late afternoon and turned back up the Clay Yard without a word about where they had been or what had been read over the top of him; the wool smelled of woodsmoke and the door did not quite shut.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. On Stone 11 touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln and at no other time, fed the household from her own dish, put the fold right without looking and gave the instruction about the draught to the fire. On Stone 12 carried the boy two doors down to a neighbour’s house for the Drawing, turned the basket with her knee and set it at the edge of the light, not where the slate lay open, and said \emph{a pot filled is a pot carried} to the girl at the hearth. Stood a half-pace from bench and bed with her burn shut on nothing and did not look toward the basket when the man gave. At dusk banked the coals under ash with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{that’ll hold} to the fire, put the fold right without looking at his face, and said nothing about where they had been, what had been taken or from whom. Did not touch the mark at the bank. Did not answer Jorra’s \emph{the back room’s cold}; shifted the damper instead. Fed the boy gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish and entered neither the spoon nor the boy.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 5: Days 7--9. Touched the widow’s mark before opening the kiln on Stone 13 and at no other time, held it a moment longer than the touch required, and gave the instruction to the fire. Fed the boy barley gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish, spoon wiped on her sleeve, and said \emph{the house}, never \emph{I}; put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and did not wipe the drool. At dusk banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark. Carried him down to the Fishstairs on Stone 8 and to the market’s edge on Stone 9, kept the half-pace from open slates and the shade where no slate lay, laid marks for two pair of eels and counted them with her eyes, and said nothing about the cuff, the cord, the crust or where they had been. On Stone 15 counted her loaves and bits with her lips twice and returned to the same place, keeping the days to Kindling as a shape and not a number; neither thanked nor refused the crust and did not take it out.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Days 10--14. On Stone 16 touched the widow’s mark before lifting the kiln lid and at no other hour, moved her lips along the loaf shelf so the days to Kindling stood as a shape, and did not touch the mark when Alda came or at the dusk bank. Kept a half-pace from the neighbour’s slate at the threshold and told her to ask the pot; let Garl’s uncalled debt lie in the space where the sentence ended. On Stone 18 said \emph{the house} and gave the neighbour the pot instead of a number; at the yard well kept the half-pace and drew water; at dusk did not touch the mark. On Stone 19 turned the coals with the back of a broken cup, called the crack in the ice weather, slid the basket a hand’s breadth out of the draught without looking at his face, measured the ridge with her thumb --- near two thumbs here, a finger more two doors down --- and said leave it, it’ll be swept on the Last Day. On Stone 20, Account-day, did not touch the mark because a reading is not an opening, carried him down in the basket and set it in the moot-post’s shade, kept a half-pace from every open slate, did not look into the basket, and carried him home through the doors going shut. Put the fold right without looking at his face, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, banked the coals with the back of a broken pot and said \emph{that’ll hold}. Neither took out nor named the cold crust Mira had put in the fold.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Days 15--24. Touched the widow’s mark before each opening (Stone 21, 25, 27, 29, 30) and at no other hour, including the bank and the reading at the last market. Counted fuel and bread into the last tend with her lips and loaves, moving three here, two there and one set apart with its brown edge turned up, and came back to it twice; answered the man who brought a number from the ice in a shut fist with \emph{It’s a cold} and fed the fire. Sent Tarn for a collector for a neighbour two doors down, carried the basket there and set it at the edge of the light away from any open slate, standing a half-pace off with her burn shut on nothing. Kept the boy’s ears out of the draught off the brook by speaking to the wool, fed him from the house’s own dish with the spoon wiped on her sleeve, and entered neither. On Stone 29 laid her thumb in the Vail ridge and then the death-house ridge and came back without saying which was which; let the debt against the tiles be circled and not named, and said Garl’s sayings to the pot and the fire. On Stone 30 carried him down for the reading with the mark untouched because a reading is not an opening, set him in the moot-post’s shade, kept her half-pace, and at dusk set the fold right without looking at his face, put him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, and banked the coals with the back of a broken pot. Neither took out nor named either crust, and said nothing about where they had been.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 25--30. On Kindling took the year’s fire in a clay dish from hands along the yard and tipped it into the kiln, touching the widow’s mark for one breath before the opening and at no other hour; nobody said where the flame came from or what it cost and she did not enter either. Fed him gruel from the house’s own dish and gave the instruction to the fire and the wool, saying \emph{the house}. Through the Five touched the mark before openings only, never at a bank; at the Weighing kept her half-pace from every open slate and did not repeat the name the clean voice read; on the Long Night let the fire go out at dusk and told the Return in the dark; at the Remembering went around Garl’s name as around Ash and let Alda lay dates where it should have stood; on the Last Day would not let anyone sweep early, measured the Vail ridge with her thumb and the neighbour’s a finger’s width thicker two doors down, and left both where they lay. On Ilmen 1 let a neighbour call the burned grey dealt while she said nothing, kept the coals banked so there was no opening and the mark stayed untouched, put the fold right without looking at his face, fed him from the house’s own dish and said nothing about where any warmth came from or who had paid.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 9: Days 31–37. At the yard well on Ilmen 2 drew her bucket with the little-door burn closing first on the rope and then on nothing, said \emph{That’ll do} to the bucket and \emph{Keep it off him; it’s the river wind} to the wool, said \emph{the house} and did not say who paid for the warmth in the household dish. On Ilmen 3 fed him gruel from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, did not wipe his mouth, and at the bank turned the coals with a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a dusk is not an opening. On Ilmen 5 stood a half-pace off while Alda reached for the slate first, laid dates where a name should stand and turned a fourth note writing-down into her shawl, and asked nothing. On Ilmen 6 touched the widow’s mark before the opening, held it one breath, let go, and did not touch it again for a pot, a note or a nearly-full sound; moved the damper after Jorra. On Ilmen 7 answered the man with the figure in his fist by speaking to the fire --- \emph{It’s a cold. That’s all it is. Feed the fire} --- and did not ask what was in the fist. On Ilmen 8 carried him three doors down and set the basket in the shade at the end of nineteen steps without looking into it, then carried him up the yard at dusk; turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and did not touch the mark, because a bank was not an opening. Neither took out nor named either crust and no third came; said nothing about the payer of any warmth.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 10: Days 38–44. On Ilmen 9 held the basket on the bank at the Slip Brook with the little-door burn shut on the wicker, turned the boy’s face toward the bank and did not set him down while the yard lifted Dessa from the clay; went to the fire afterward and sent nobody toward the road for a collector, and did not name the omission. Gave the instruction to the wool and the pot, said \emph{the house}, did not touch the widow’s mark because there had been no opening. On Ilmen 11 laid her thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash had turned and then in the ridge two doors down, brought it back without saying which was which and fetched no broom; fed him from the house’s own dish and left both crusts where they lay. On Ilmen 12 kept a half-pace from the eel-board and the writing at the gate. On Ilmen 13 carried a clay jar from House Silt, held the basket level inside the door a finger’s width open, opened no slate and set the jar on the shelf by the wall at home. On Ilmen 14 and 15 carried him upriver to the Weir, left him in the shade out of the draught, stood a half-pace from a slate under a woman’s arm on the way back, and at dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face. Still had not said who paid for the warmth or that the woman in the brook was the mother of the child under her roof.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 11: Days 45–47. Carried him below the north bridge at dawn and up the Clay Yard at dusk, setting him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right without looking at his face; every instruction to the fire, the pot and the wool, and the house where another woman would say I. Touched the widow’s mark once before opening the kiln on Day 45 and at no other hour, not at any bank. Went around the month in loaves and glances, moved a loaf along the shelf and came back to the same place, glanced at the clay jar on the wall shelf, and let nobody say the stores were thinner. Fed him gruel thinned with milk from the house’s own dish with two fingers behind his ear, wiped the spoon on her sleeve and did not wipe his mouth. At the well kept a half-pace from every open slate, went wide around a slate at the rack end and gave the instruction to the bucket; told a neighbour the house had sent the number up the road. Did not touch the mark at the dusk banks and did not name either the payer of the warmth or the crust that went out of the fold. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 12: Days 48–54. At the well she told the fire it was the thaw and gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket, never to the basket, saying the house; she went at a half-pace from every open slate and around a slate propped at the rack end, and did not touch the widow’s mark because a well is not an opening. On Account-day she set the basket in the moot-post’s shade and carried him home without a word about the figure read over him. Each dusk she set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, and put the fold right without looking at his face. She stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote a fifth note and did not ask what was written, and said nothing about the payer of the milk, the payer of any warmth, or the crust that went out of the fold on Day 46. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 13: Days 55--60. On Ilmen 26 at the yard well told the fire it was the thaw when a man come downriver from Greybank spoke of a counting room shut in the last war with the damper closed and men dead of the breath, and did not connect it to the Vail kiln (T065); touched no mark, because a well and a story over a bucket are not openings. On Ilmen 27 carried the basket three doors down into House Silt, set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, opened no slate, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row, stood a half-pace off while Alda laid the slates writing-down and pressed the fold too long, and asked nothing (T058, T084). Through the days gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket, never to the basket, said the house, and kept the days to Silt in loaves, glances and an uncalled space at the shelf’s end. On Ilmen 29 laid one thumb in the clean dark line where the Ash ridge turned and the same thumb in the ridge two doors down, a finger’s width wider, and brought the knowledge back without saying which was which and without fetching a broom (T013, T009). At the last market kept the half-pace and carried him home at dusk with one crust and an empty place in the fold. On Silt 1 stood over the new hairline of grey in the corner with a broom in her hand and did not sweep, telling the fire it was the thaw and would go when it goes; touched the widow’s mark before the opening and at no other hour; kept the carried fire under blind ash and broken pot at four, four and a gap; set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and said nothing about the river beginning to move under the ice.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 14: Days 61–67. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and kept her half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the well. Told the fire it was the thaw when the brook came up clay-heavy and when the ice was honeyed all through; left the new finer grey beside the clean dark line unswept. No opening came in seven days and she did not touch the widow’s mark once. On Silt 5 carried the basket three doors down, set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote and asked nothing. Each dusk set him on his bed under the roof, not in the Debt Loft, and put the fold right without looking at his face, carrying one crust and an empty place through seven days unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 15: Days 68–74, Silt 9–15. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool and the bucket and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and kept the half-pace from every open slate at the Fishstairs, the Cross, the racks and three doors down.
