Carried him to the edge of the thin brown sheet and back; told the fire it was the thaw when a neighbour said the house had been saved and did not say it herself. Stood over the clean dark line and the new finer grey with a broom and swept neither, and gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around}); went wide around the space under the lowest rack. Touched the widow’s mark at no hour in seven days, because no opening came at a rack, a shore, a step, a door or a bed. On Silt 13 carried him three doors down and back with the door a finger’s width open and opened no slate, asking nothing about the sixth page or the tin. Did not go down to the child in the yard whose foot stayed cold, and the boy did not lay it beside the child of hers who cooled while everybody was kind. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one crust stiff in the fold with the empty place unnamed. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 16: Days 75–77, Silt 16–18. Kept the house through the mud the flood left: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and the half-pace from every open slate at the racks, the well, the Fishstairs and House Silt. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the finer grey and the space under the lowest rack with neither line swept; told the fire it was the thaw. Told a woman who wanted a figure to ask the pot what a wet thing costs, and did not say the house was saved. At the well went wide around a slate set out to dry, did not touch the widow’s mark, and did not look at the foundling in cast-offs, his green sliver or the warm loaf in his pocket, and did not connect the man from Slate Row with either. No opening came in three days and the mark was not touched. Carried him up at dusk each day, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped; one stiff crust and its unnamed empty place. The private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 17: Days 78–84, Silt 19–25. Kept the house through the lean week: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the well, the Cross, House Silt and the racks. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them and telling the fire it was the thaw. At the yard well on Silt 25 heard the second man from Greybank tell the bucket-round of the counting room shut in the war with the damper closed and the men dead of the breath; told the fire it was the thaw, made nothing of it and did not join it to her roof. Carried the boy three doors down on Silt 21, set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from any open slate, opened none and turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row, and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid the slates down before the fold and wrote what she would not show. Let Jorra’s dust and his finger at the damper pass unasked, let Tarn’s six counted and seventh held stand as the house’s one unchecked entry. No opening came in seven days and the widow’s mark was not touched; the private roll stayed unshown. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped, one brown-edged crust with the empty place beside it still unnamed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 18: Days 85–90, Silt 26–30 and Seed 1. Kept the house through the turning of the month: every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket, \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, the half-pace from every open slate at the yard, the well, the racks, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody on Silt 26 and Seed 1 and went around the boot-print in the brown skin, the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them and telling the fire it was the thaw. To the woman who asked what the month would cost moved her lips along the loaf shelf, glanced at the clay jar and said to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there; put no figure to the space at the row’s end and let a man say the strips east of town would want hands by the morrow without giving the hands or the strips a number. When the shut-room story went over the bucket again told the fire it was the thaw and joined nothing to her roof. Three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long and wrote what she would not show. On Silt 30 set him in the moot-post’s thin shade with cold iron at his cheek while Berr read one in twelve over fewer bodies, carried him home at dusk and said nothing about what had been read over him. Jorra’s dust and his damper ahead of her sentence, Tarn’s six counted and seventh held, Alda’s tin and Berr’s box all stayed as they were; no opening came in six days and a month’s turning was not one, so the widow’s mark was not touched. The private roll stayed unshown and the empty place at the row’s end stayed unnamed. At dusk set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without a look at his face and left the thread at his mouth frozen and unwiped, one crust and its unnamed empty place carried into Seed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 19: Days 91–93. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the strips east of Low Kiln, the Clay Yard, the yard well, the Fishstairs and House Silt, and set him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket and the broom and never to the basket; gave the broom its instruction before anybody --- \emph{Round it. The month’s for planting and there’s nothing planted here. It cost enough to come in; it’ll cost more to take out} --- and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack, sweeping none of them. On Seed 2 told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and, to a woman who asked what the planting would cost, moved her lips along the loaf shelf, glanced at the clay jar, left the empty place at the row’s end with no figure and said \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there} and \emph{the house has said it}. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days; its payer had gone unnamed for ninety-three days and the coal the gull took was entered in no slate. Did not touch the widow’s mark at a strip, a broom, a well, a market, a door or a bed, because none was an opening. Three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long. At the close put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; one brown-edged crust lay stiff in the fold with the empty place unnamed and no third.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 20: Days 94–100, Seed 5–11, the planting become waiting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate in the strips, the Clay Yard, the yard well, House Silt, the Fishstairs, the Cross and under the roof, setting him on his bed each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the fire, the wool, the bucket, the broom and the pot and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 5 told a woman at the well to ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there because \emph{the house has said it}; on Seed 6 moved her lips along a loaf row that now stood with two empty places and said nothing about either, while a neighbour’s hand passed over the new gap and went on with her pot. Told the fire it was the thaw on all seven days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and kept its payer unnamed for a hundred days. Did not go down to the child below the sill whose foot stayed cold, though it is told of her in the yard that she once sat three nights with a child of her own who cooled while everybody was kind; she has never told that story herself and would not describe it that way. At the close put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, and did not touch the widow’s mark because no opening came. The two shelf gaps and the empty place in the fold stayed in rooms that do not touch and were not named, joined or solved; the private roll stayed unshown.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 21: Days 101–103, Seed 12–14, the third week of the planting become waiting. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate in the Clay Yard, at the loaf shelf, at the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof each dusk and not in the Debt Loft. Gave every instruction to the pot, the fire, the broom, the wool and the water and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, told the fire it was the thaw on all three days and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and three days. On Seed 12 moved her lips along a loaf row that stood with two empty places, glanced at the clay jar and left both gaps unfigured while a neighbour named them in one breath as a planting and an appetite; she did not join them. Gave the broom its instruction before anybody and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 13 said \emph{Yes, house} to an early thaw and a late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying; stood a half-pace off while Alda wrote three doors down, and did not ask about the writing or the tin. On Seed 14 carried him down to the eels, set the basket where no slate lay, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down, away from every open slate, opening none. At dusk put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; touched the widow’s mark at no hour, because a shelf, a strip, a basket, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 22: Days 104–106, Seed 15–17, the hands at last going into the strips. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips east of Low Kiln, the loaf shelf, the wheel-shed, the yard well, the Fishstairs and three doors down in House Silt, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at dusk each day. Gave the instruction to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gave the broom its instruction before anybody (\emph{Go around. It cost enough to come in. It’ll cost more to take out}) and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 15 moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour said the old space at the end came in with the planting and went off with her pot; she did not join the two tellings. Told the fire it was the thaw and turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, its payer unnamed for a hundred and four days; the fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been. On Seed 16 said \emph{Yes, house} to the early and late thaw and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying, stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, and gave the house no name for the men. On Seed 17 set the basket at the very end of the fish-trade shade, told the wool and the water and never the basket, and midday set it just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down away from every open slate, opening none and turning no errand into a walk to Slate Row; said nothing about the writing, the tin or the fold pressed too long. At dusk put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; touched the widow’s mark at no hour, because a strip, a shelf, a rack, a well, a market, a door and a bed are not openings. The private roll stayed unshown, the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed apart and unnamed with no third, and no bond changed hands, no tin or box opened and no new scar or possession.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 23: Days 107–109, Seed 18–20, the planting month entering its last tend. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the yard well, the wheel-shed, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, the Cross and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft at dusk each day. Gave the instruction to the broom, the bucket, the wool, the water, the pot and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, gave the broom its instruction before she gave it to anybody (\emph{Over the road first, then the Clay Yard, and let the line lie where it lies}), and went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw and the space under the lowest rack without sweeping any of them. On Seed 18 three doors down set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. At the loaf shelf that afternoon moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar and gave nobody a figure while a neighbour called the old gap a thing the planting brought in and went off with her pot without seeing the empty place at his ear; did not join the two tellings. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot and fed it, the fire answering four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nine days; stood a moment at the fire with the back of the broken pot in her hand counting something under her breath, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 18 said \emph{Yes, house} to those who wanted the thaw early and those who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. On Seed 19 stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, giving the house no name for them; told the fire it was the thaw and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a wheel-shed, a rack, a yard and a basket are not openings. On Seed 20 set the basket in the moot-post’s thin shade before the crowd thickened, gave the instruction to the wool and the wind and never to the basket, kept her half-pace from every open slate and carried him home at dusk saying nothing about the figure read over the strips. Touched the widow’s mark at no hour and kept her private roll unshown; put the fold right without looking at his face and left the thread frozen; one stiff crust and its unnamed empty place, the shelf’s two gaps in the other room, no third. No new scar or possession; the grey streak at her temple is more marked.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 24: Days 110–112, Seed 21–23, the last tend of the planting. At the loaf shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced at the clay jar cold under its glaze and let a neighbour reach past the bare board and go off naming the old gap a planting and the new one the price of a wet thing without joining the two sayings or touching the widow’s mark. At the well on Seed 22 sent a woman who asked what the planting cost to the pot: \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it.} Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}; stood a moment with the back of the pot in her hand counting something under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the burn, the grey streak pale at her temple, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 22 gave the broom its instruction before anybody and Tarn took it up; men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, the household straightening around his silence, and she gave the end of it to the pot. His broom checked half a beat behind the standing finger and went on, and she asked nothing about either. At the Fishstairs and three doors down set the basket where no slate lay and opened none, standing a half-pace off; said nothing about the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. The carried fire kept four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and twelve days. No opening came in three days, the widow’s mark hung where it hung and the private roll stayed unshown; one crust in the fold and two shelf gaps in another room were not named, joined or solved.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

Gave the instruction to the bucket, the broom, the pot, the wool, the water and the fire before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, moved her lips along a loaf row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and gave nobody a figure. At the shelf on Seed 24 sent a woman with wet sleeves to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and heard a neighbour call the old gap a planting and the child’s empty place an appetite in one breath without joining the two or touching the widow’s mark. Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 25 stood a half-pace off while men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and the household straightened around his silence. Tarn took the broom only after its instruction and his stroke went on without the half-check of the day before, the flagstones keeping the stopped place; she asked nothing about either. Three doors down at midday set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. At the Fishstairs and the Cross on Seed 26 set the basket where no slate lay and opened none. No opening came in three days and the widow’s mark stayed untouched; the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 26: Days 116–119, Seed 27–30, the planting month ending and Reed coming on. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the worked strips, the wheel-shed’s edge of light, the stalls beyond the Cross, the yard well, the loaf shelf, the Fishstairs, House Silt and the moot-post’s shade, setting him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each going of the light, putting the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and leaving the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed before it went away. Gave the instruction to the bucket, broom, pot, fire, wool, water and wind before anybody and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, held the basket level the way a woman carries a bowl filled to the lip, and went around the empty place in the returning line, the space beneath the lowest rack and the clean dark line as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering none of them. At the loaf shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf is not an opening; she heard neighbours on Seed 27 and Seed 29 lay two bare boards under one appetite in a single breath and did not join the sayings or the two absences. The house has said it.} Told the fire it was the thaw on all four days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the wrist that carries the little-door burn, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and did not look toward the bed. On Seed 28 men unnamed came before first grey and Jorra’s bent finger went into the damper ahead of her unfinished sentence; she gave the end of it to the pot and asked nothing about the dust or the men. With Tarn the exact account held — six counted, the seventh nearly gone and held at the edge of the sill, the breath from Seed 16 unspent, the unchecking stroke beside the earlier half-beat — and she asked about neither. Three doors down at midday she set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door away from every open slate, opened none, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda pressed the fold too long; said nothing of the writing, the tin or the date over the sign. The carried fire answered four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and nineteen days. No opening came in four days, the widow’s mark hung where it hung, the private roll stayed unshown and the two shelf gaps and the fold’s gap stayed apart and unnamed. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

Gave every instruction to the bucket, broom, pot, fire, wool and river wind and never to the basket, said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and sent a woman who asked what the reeds would cost to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. Went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called thaw, the space under the lowest rack and the missing hand’s place in the strip as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it, entering none of them (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). At the shelf moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, gave nobody a figure and did not touch the widow’s mark, because a shelf, a strip, a rack, a market and a bed are not openings (T060/T086). On all three days told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, fed them and said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, standing a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushing a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, and not looking toward the bed; its payer went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-two days (T088). On Reed 2 gave the men unnamed before first grey no name and let Jorra’s bent finger stand in the cold damper ahead of her unfinished sentence, giving the end of it to the pot (T035/T031/T062), and let Tarn’s stroke go on over the flagstones without the half-check while the stones kept the stopped place, asking about neither (T036/T076). No opening came in three days, the private roll stayed unshown, the two shelf gaps and the fold’s one crust stayed in rooms that do not touch, and she has still not said whose child he is.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 28: Days 123–125, Reed 4–6. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the yard, the strips’ edge, the Weir, the Cross and back under the roof, set him on his bed each dusk and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting needed. Gave the instruction to the wool, wind, bucket, broom, pot and fire and never the basket; said \emph{the house}; went wide around the rack space and the missing hand’s place; sent a woman asking the reeds’ cost to the pot with \emph{the house has said it} and glanced once at the clay jar. Moved her lips along a shelf standing with two gaps and gave nobody a figure. Told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed a strand of coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, and set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand without looking toward the bed. Asked nothing about the men unnamed, Jorra’s finger in the damper, his dust, Tarn’s near-saying or his seventh year. Widow’s mark untouched; payer of the carried fire’s fifth breath unnamed for a hundred and twenty-five days. No new scar or possession.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 29: Days 126–128, Reed 7–9. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the stalls beyond the Cross, the Weir, House Silt three doors down and back under the roof, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each dusk, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and left the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting each night. Gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the bucket, the broom, the pot and the fire and never to the basket; said \emph{the house}; went around the clean dark line, the finer hairline called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates and the place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back, as wide as a pail of hot water set where a child might knock it (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). A woman who asked what the reeds would cost was sent to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. At the Cross on Day 126 set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay and stood a half-pace off; kept half a pace from a woman come near with a slate under her arm. Three doors down on Day 128 set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, opened no slate, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid her birth-slates before the fold, asked nothing about the sign, the date, the tin or the six pages. At the fire on all three days told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and did not look toward the bed; the payer went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-eight days (T088). Within hearing of Tarn’s second stopping she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; she did not ask Jorra about the men, his dust or his finger in the damper, and neither man named the other’s silence. Widow’s mark untouched at a shelf, an afternoon, a strip, a rack, a basket, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and nothing was explained.

Went wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the broken birth-slates under the lowest rack and the place in the returning line where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). On Day 141 a neighbour reached past the bare board with her hand before her eyes and named the old shelf-gap and the empty place at the boy’s ear under one appetite in a single breath; Sella heard and did not join either, sent her to the pot, moved her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and, standing with her back to the basket, reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies without looking and without a word, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread; T097 advanced, not paid). \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 35: Days 144–146, Reed 25–27, the reed month going out. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the loaf shelf and hearth, the wheel-shed’s edge, the Weir and House Silt three doors down, setting him on his bed under the roof each going of the light and not in the Debt Loft, putting the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, leaving the thread of drool frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it went away. Gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, said \emph{the house}, and sent a woman who asked what the hands would be paid to the weather and the river with no figure. On Day 144 stood with her back to the basket, moved her lips along a row standing with two gaps, glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze and reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread). Told the fire it was the thaw on all three days, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood a moment counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, and set the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand. On Day 145 gave the house no name to the men who came low into the back room before first grey, did not say the room was cold, and did not ask Jorra about his dust or the damper; within hearing of Tarn’s \textbf{eighth} stopping she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing, and neither man named the other’s silence. On Day 146 set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door three doors down and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid her birth-slates before the fold, crossed the flower unknowing, covered it with \emph{Stone seven. The account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, said \emph{Warm and breathing} exact and not true and touched her tin unopened; she asked nothing about the writing, the tin, the sign or the date. At the close she went around the pan set out to dry and the iced trough, left the widow’s mark untouched because a dusk is not an opening, and went to her own bed without explaining the count. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 36: Days 147–149, Reed 28–30, on stage all three days. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the reed beds, the Vail kiln-house, the wheel-shed’s edge, the Weir and the last market at the Cross, and up the clay road at the going of the light, giving the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket, saying \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}, and telling the fire it was the thaw. To a girl with a creel and to a man who asked what the hands would be paid she gave the weather and the river, never a figure; to the recurring woman who came up from the strips with a wet pot and asked what the row would want she gave \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, and the woman carried the unanswered question away level so nothing slopped (T058/T079, T077). Went wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the space beneath the lowest rack with its broken birth-slates and the empty place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come out, with a look and a wide step and no number (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). On Day 147, standing with her back to the basket and moving her lips along the row with its two unnamed gaps, she glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, reached a finger BENEATH the front edge where the charcoal tally lies without looking and without a word, brought it away and did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unread). On Day 148, before first grey, men unnamed went low into the room off the shed; she carried him past at the half-pace, turned no head toward the door, gave the house no name for them and did not say the room was cold, and within hearing of Tarn’s \textbf{ninth} stopping gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing (T035/T031, T036/T076). On all three days she turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale off the coals, and set the pot rim out with its handle two inches beyond the reaching hand; neither looked toward the bed nor touched the widow’s mark at a shelf, an afternoon, a market or a dusk, because none was an opening. At the last market she set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and kept the half-pace from every open slate while the square sold over the clerk and a sixth green and a sixth half-turn stood unread; she made nothing of either and joined nothing. At the going of the light on Day 149 she carried him up the clay road around the pan and the trough with its skin of ice, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face, left the thread of drool frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it went away, told the fire it was the thaw, said \emph{The house will keep it} and went to her own bed without explaining the count; the two rooms did not touch. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, nothing explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 37: Days 150–152, Tallow 1–3, Firstday to Thirdday, on stage all three days. On Day 150 at the kiln mouth she performed the chapter’s one meaningful change --- the first opening of the month --- touching the widow’s mark before the kiln, holding it one breath and letting go, then tipping the coal under a broken pot and going back to setting pots, with the rule holding exactly at every shelf, well, afternoon and dusk that followed (T058/T079). Through the three days she carried the boy at the half-pace from every open slate, gave the instruction to wool, fire, pot, broom and running water and never to the basket, went around the pan’s gone place, the trough without its ice and wide around the rack space with the broken birth-slates, told the fire it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, set the pot handle two inches beyond the hand that could not close on it and left the mark hanging where it hung at a dusk. On Day 151 at the Weir she gave a cost asked as a direction back as a direction (T077), and at the shelf, standing with her back to the basket, reached a finger beneath the board where the charcoal tally lies without looking or a word (T100 carried, unread). On Day 152, with men unnamed in the back room and Jorra’s finger leading at the damper, she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing while Tarn’s ear-sentence stopped short of the threshold with no tenth standing (T035/T031, T036/T076, T065/T095); the fire’s payer was unnamed for a hundred and fifty-two days (T088). No bond changed hands, no tin or box opened, no secret entered.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

At the going of the light on all three days she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke going before her and the river wind behind, set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, put the fold right without looking at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, let her hand rest a half-beat longer than the setting needed, and went to her own bed; the two rooms did not touch. The two rooms did not touch. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands, no secret entered.

Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate; gave the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom and the running water and never to the basket; said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}; set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting; and kept the widow’s mark where it hung at every shelf, well, rack, road, basket, afternoon and dusk, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour (T058/T079). The house has said it}, and the woman carried the question away level with nothing slopped, priced, refused or entered (T077). \textbf{The chapter’s one meaningful change, paid small and non-fatally:} on Day 188 a rack-worker’s pot gave its high thin note before its time and then sang itself out early, and the woman went on with her hands and made no lesson of it; two men then carried a glaze-room hand out of the kiln and across the yard toward the clay road, alive and breathing, sweet-sickness on his breath, the pale line at his gum, his own hand limp with fingers the colour of old rope and pewter-pale nails, one carrier’s thumb hooked under his arm to keep the head from lopping. She set the basket down at the yard’s edge, turned his face as she would turn a pot so the light fell where she wanted it, went wide around the place the carriers crossed with a look that asked for nothing and found nothing, and gave the yard no name for what ailed him; no collector called, no figure given, no payer named and no slate opened, and the cost stayed entered nowhere (T077 advanced, not paid as a thread). At the going of the light each day she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before and river wind behind, going wide around the pan’s gone place, the bare dark trough, the rack space and the field’s empty place, and set him on his bed and not in the Debt Loft, base first and the weight settled as a woman sets a vessel that must not rock, the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and the thread frozen and unwiped (T058/T079). She moved her lips along the loaf row with its two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, kept her finger from beneath the front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100 carried), and glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without a touch. When her instruction went low and unfinished at the hearth on all three days Jorra’s bent finger stood in the cold damper until the sentence reached the pot; the fraction stayed held and unspoken, a remembered holding on the second and third days and not a new change, not paired with the Day 166 beat or the Day 171 flagstone half-check into a rule with a payer (T062). While the finger stood Tarn’s stroke went on over the flagstones without the half-check and neither man named the other’s silence (T036/T076). Three or four unnamed men went low into the back room before first grey on Day 187 and she gave them no name and did not say the room was cold; the two shut-room tellings stayed two with no third (T035/T031, T065/T095). No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no opening and no bond paid.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 46: Days 189, 190 and 191, Ember 10–12, Tenthday to Secondday, on stage on all three days. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate; gave the instruction to the wool, the fire, the pot, the broom, the running water and the river wind and never to the basket; said \emph{the house} where another woman would say \emph{I}; set the pot handle two inches beyond the reaching hand with the half-beat at setting; and kept the widow’s mark where it hung at every morning, shelf, well, rack, road, basket, yard, afternoon and dusk, because the one opening was before the kiln on Ember 1 and the hand goes to the mark at no other hour (T058/T079). Fed the fire under a broken pot: four low pulls and the silence where the fifth should have been, its payer unnamed for a hundred and eighty-nine, a hundred and ninety and a hundred and ninety-one days; told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist so the grey streak showed pale, and glanced once at the clay jar cold under its glaze without touching it. On Day 189 she carried him down to the Cross and set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay, then stood half a pace off through Berr’s reading — \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says}, \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}, \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — and the bell’s four, four and a gap, giving no instruction or reason to the basket (T015/T041/T047/T077, T078). On Days 190 and 191 she sent women who asked what the firing would cost to the pot and the weather with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, carried the questions away level, and went wide around the clean dark line, the finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates, the pan’s gone ring, the bare trough, the field’s empty place and the place the carriers crossed, with a look and a wide step and no number (T077, T009/T013/T092/T098). She moved her lips along the loaf row with its two unnamed gaps and gave nobody a figure, and kept her finger from beneath the front edge so the charcoal stayed unread, uncounted and uncopied (T100 carried). At the going of the light each day she carried him home up the clay road, woodsmoke before and river wind behind, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft, base first, the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face and the thread left frozen, her hand resting a half-beat longer at the setting, and went to her own bed; the two rooms did not touch. With Jorra the holdings at the damper on all three days were remembered repetitions and not new changes; with Tarn the ear-sentence stayed short of the word, the ninth stopping had no tenth and the two silences stayed unjoined. Hessa’s inward slate, the clerk’s measure, the green-mouthed woman and the foundling stayed offstage after the market. The reading did not answer the man carried out on Day 188 and the cost stayed entered nowhere. No new scar or possession, no change of voice, no opening and no bond paid.

\end{itemize}
}

\CRcharacter*{Berr Clay}{the man who signs the levy in a neat hand}{build/art/characters/berr-clay.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Berr, Berr Clay of the Cross, the Thane of Clay, the Thane}\CRfield{Role}{antagonist}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 764, High Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{High Kiln, Sill, Grath; a kiln-master’s house}\CRfield{Allegiance}{Kiln-Masters of Sill; Thane of Clay, confirmed by the Court’s factor at Greybank}\CRfield{Status}{alive — the box still locked up the clay road at the close of Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month; last seen that morning coming up short off the clay road to the reading block with the red wool cord of his office folded square under his coat and the green of tasted lead glaze at one mouth-corner, wiping his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, holding a narrow slate unopened to his forearm, passing a finger over the figure, reading \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the goers-by, saying \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me} and \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, and going off toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true subtraction inside, believing he has done a kindness; the printed figure stands unchallenged and a figure read aloud is still not the figure paid; he was not called for the glaze-room hand carried out on Day 188}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 3}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Forty-eight, heavy in the way a wagoner is heavy, with a back that has carried clay and a grey stubble he trims with a knife before market-day. He has a ring of lead-glaze green at the corner of his mouth from the old kiln-master’s habit of tasting glaze, and he cannot stop doing it in front of people, which the masters read as thoroughness and Sella reads as nerves. He wears a cord of red wool across his chest when he sits as Thane and takes it off before he goes home, folding it into a drawer. His hands are large and clean; he wipes his thumb on his apron before he touches a slate so that the slate will stay clean. He smells of hot clay, lead and, on Court business, nothing at all, which is the most expensive smell in Grath.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
The kiln-master’s proverb braided with the Court’s passive grammar. He never says \emph{I} when he can say \emph{the district} or \emph{the account}, and he never raises his voice, which in a moot is more frightening than shouting because the crowd has to lean in to hear him. He apologises in the form of an instruction. He uses the phrase \emph{as the notice says} the way another man might cross himself.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “The levy is called. It is not called by me.”

\item “One in twelve, as the notice says. If your household has heard otherwise, your household has heard wrong.”

\item “You can bring the slate to the moot. The moot will shout. The slate will not change.”

\item “Sella. Your widow’s mark is confirmed by the factor at Greybank. That is a kindness, and kindness is entered.”

\item “I signed for the Hearth. I did not sign for a name. There’s a difference, and you can take it to the Cross if you like.”

\item “The figure stands as read. There’ll be a slate at the watch if the house wants it again.”

\item “A number goes into a slate, not a bundle. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch.” --- at the eel stall on Reed 18, with the red cord folded under his coat and the true subtraction in the locked box.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in High Kiln, the son of a glaze-mixer, and worked up through the yards until the masters chose him Thane of Clay and the Court’s factor at Greybank confirmed it, which is the only way a Thane is confirmed. He has kept the Sill kilns firing through two bad winters and a war of deductions that he describes, when pressed, as \emph{a disagreement about arithmetic}. In Y.H. 811, when the Long Cold had the district calling itself walking thin, he raised the levy to one in three on the factor’s instruction and announced it as one in twelve, because the printed notices say one in twelve and the notices are what a man can be seen reading. He has read the difference in a locked box in his own house. He has never destroyed the box.

In the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812, he signed the slate that took forty children of Low Kiln for a private account. The factor at Greybank showed him the purchaser’s name and Berr has forgotten it on purpose, which is a thing a man can do if he is sufficiently determined and sufficiently afraid. He told the district the warmth was for the Hearth, and to a mother named Dessa Silt he said one in twelve and meant one in three. His daughter came back thin in Y.H. 800 and does not remember him; he has kept her name on a slate at home and has never corrected the deduction on her return, because the return is what the household was given and a household does not look a gift in the mouth.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
A daughter who calls him by another man’s name when she is feverish. He fears being seen clearly by Sella, who knew his wife and knows the difference between a levy and a theft. He fears that the locked box will outlive him and that his son will open it. He fears, most of all, that the district will one day ask him why forty children were necessary when one intact measure should have served, because he has an answer ready and knows it will not balance. His contradiction: the man who counts warmth as a public good has privately bought a whole return for his granddaughter and paid for it with the deduction from Low Kiln, and calls the purchase \emph{a gift from the Hearth}.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants the kilns firing, his name on the roll, and the factor at Greybank to write back in the same hand next year. He thinks he wants the Court’s confirmation. What he needs is to learn that he is the most frightening thing in Sarn — not a dark lord, but a reasonable man with a ledger and a good reason — and that the reason is the part that will be remembered against him.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Sella Vail} — he confirmed her widow’s mark and has never called in the debt Garl left against a shipment of tiles. The uncalled debt is worse than a called one: she cannot pay it, cannot settle it, and cannot stop owing it. She has never asked, and he has decided this means she knows. \emph{Ch 3:} he told her at the Cross that the mark was confirmed by the factor at Greybank, that it was a kindness, and that kindness is entered. She answered the wool and the boy, not him; he stood with his mouth open on the next part of what he had come to say, looked at the mark under her collar without asking to see it, and went back to the moot leaving the debt as carefully unentered as he had found it.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — he suspects the young man is with the Broken Slates and lets him be. A district needs somewhere to put its anger, and Berr has calculated that a kiln-house with a safe place for anger is cheaper than a kiln-house without one. Jorra threw a stone at his door in Y.H. 810; Berr had the stone swept up and does not mention it.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — dead friend and rival. Berr let the Vail house carry a debt rather than call it in, and has spent a year being unable to decide whether this was mercy or the simplest way to keep a witness quiet. \emph{Ch 3:} the debt against the firing of tiles went spoken around at the Cross, a space in a sentence shaped like the hollow seat up the yard; his care not to call it was another kindness entered nowhere.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — he pays her to keep the birth-slates and has never asked about the second notes. He has concluded that she must be paid enough not to keep them, which is an expensive conclusion and a wrong one. \emph{Ch 3:} she kept the birth-slates in a row at the edge of the market, turning the writing down when a mother came near; he did not see the crossed sign she made at the boy’s wrist or the date she covered it with, which is the whole point of paying someone to keep a record.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he took one in three from her wages and told her one in twelve. She spat at his door and denied it; he had the spittle cleaned before the market opened and never said who did it.

\textbf{Corin} — he watches the boy with a kiln-master’s eye and has decided he is worth more than he costs, which is exactly how the Court will one day see him. This is not cruelty in Berr’s account. It is an investment. \emph{Ch 3:} the boy lay in a basket at the edge of his square all morning and he never once looked into it. The figure was read over the top of him twice; the district went back to the pigs. He has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind.

\textbf{Ch 5.} At the Fishstairs on Stone 14 he came down the steps with the red wool cord folded under his coat and wiped his thumb on his apron before touching his slate, the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth. He said \emph{the levy is called for the feast; it is not called by me}, accepted four eels where six should go without appearing to count them, and gave out \emph{three days to the Five} from the top of the steps with a finger passed over the figure. He has paid her two marks short for six years and taken two eels short for six years, and the war has never been named by either of them. The box in his house stays locked; the true deduction stays in it.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 20, Account-day, he came to the block with the red cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching the slate, and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} low into the top of two hundred leaning people. He called the levy for the feast and said it was not called by him, passed a finger over the figure, confirmed the fire and the widow’s mark under this roof, and went around the consignment of tiles where a debt might have stood, the way a woman goes around Ash left in a corner. He did not look into the basket and went back to the pigs by dusk believing his own sentences. The box stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 30, the year’s last Account-day, he came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching the slate and read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the crowd at the last market of the year. He passed a finger over the figure, said the levy was called for the feast and was not called by him, went around the uncalled debt against the firing of tiles as carefully as Sella went around Ash in a corner, and did not look into the basket. He gave out that the Five were three days off while the district argued three, two and whatever the moot had already decided to pay, and went back to the pigs by dusk believing he had done the district a kindness. The box in his house stays locked and the true deduction stays in it.

\textbf{Ch 8.} At the Weighing on Day 26 he was glimpsed at the edge of the reading with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green glaze at one corner of his mouth; he wiped his thumb before he touched his slate, passed a finger over the figure, read a name the household would not repeat, explained nothing, looked nowhere near the basket and went off with the box in his house still locked. The clean voice in a temple’s clothes that read the measures was the same grammar of his Cross, now in an officer’s mouth, and a whole return was announced for somebody not in the room. One in twelve stayed printed and unchallenged at the Opening of the Slates on Ilmen 1 and the true deduction was spoken by nobody.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 7 he came back from the river with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it, and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before he touched nothing, passed a finger across a figure on a narrow slate, and had a number he did not care to give. When a neighbour at the well started to ask, he said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If your house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, not \emph{my account}, taking himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a man takes his hand out of a field before the dressing goes on. He went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and looked nowhere near the basket. The boy put the twice-wiped thumb on the tray where the other record-first hands lay and did not call it the same hand.

\textbf{Ch 10.} On Account-day, the day after a woman goes into the brook uncollected, he comes to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching anything and reads one in twelve \emph{as the notice says} low into the crowd. The true subtraction goes over the top of the basket and is spoken by nobody. To a neighbour who begins to ask about the thaw he says \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. If your house wants it, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- \emph{your house}, not \emph{my account} --- and takes himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand out of a field. The number for what the thaw will cost goes from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and is never given, and he goes off with the box in his house still locked and his good reason intact. He is not at the Weir for the blessing. The clerk at the Court’s table and the clerk set at the Fishstairs for an uncalled measure both put hand to slate before eye to person, and the boy files their order beside Berr’s twice-wiped thumb without calling the three the same hand.

\textbf{Ch 11.} He came up the yard on Day 47 with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay under the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over what was written and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well. The house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} --- the house, not my account; he took himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a surgeon takes a hand out of a field. He never looked into the basket and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. The figure that went from fist to mouth to shoulder went with him into a slate and stayed there.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Account-day at the Cross he wiped his thumb twice, read one in twelve twice over the basket and put himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}; the true subtraction went over the basket and the number for the thaw went from fist to mouth to shoulder and reached nobody. Sella’s widow’s mark and the uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched, Jorra’s dust was not spoken of, and Alda’s birth-slates were kept where they belonged. He never looked into the basket and went off toward High Kiln believing he had done the district a kindness, with the box still locked and the true deduction inside.

\textbf{Ch 13.} On Ilmen 30, the last Account-day and market before Silt, he came to the block with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wiped his thumb twice before touching nothing and read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} twice over the basket. He called the levy for Silt and took himself out of his own sentence with \emph{there’ll be a slate at the watch}. The true subtraction went over the basket and was spoken by nobody; the number for what the thaw and the flood would cost went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere. The bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs was glimpsed with his hand to the slate before his eyes to the stalls and did not speak. Berr went off toward High Kiln believing he had done the district a kindness, with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 2 he came up short at the outer edge of the Fishstairs shade, the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay over the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over what was written and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a well,} he said. \emph{If the house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch.} He took himself out of his own sentence as neatly as a hand out of a field before the dressing goes on, never said \emph{I}, never looked into the basket, and went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside. The eel figure went over the basket into the noise of the stalls and was gone; the boy filed the twice-wiped thumb on its own tray and did not join it to the Fishstairs clerk’s hand or to the other record-first hands.

\textbf{Ch 15.} On Silt 10, Account-day, he came up short at the edge of the dry step with water sitting on the one below it, the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat, green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth and hot clay under the smell of nothing at all. He wiped his thumb twice before he touched nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passed a finger over what was written and let his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required, then read \emph{one in twelve, as the notice says} over the water and the basket and took himself out of his own sentence, never saying \emph{I} and never looking into the basket. The true subtraction went over it unspoken and the number for what the flood would cost went from a fist to a mouth to a shoulder and arrived nowhere; the bell went four, four and a gap and nobody crossed himself. Word came up that the soft-cuffed clerk was still set at the Fishstairs with a slate for a measure nobody called, and the boy put Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or to any of the other record-first hands. Berr went off toward High Kiln with the box in his house still locked and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 20, Account-day, he comes to the block with the red wool cord folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, wipes his thumb twice before touching nothing and reads one in twelve over a crowd made thinner by the flood and the lean week. He takes himself out of his own sentence and goes off toward High Kiln believing he has done a kindness, the true subtraction locked in his box and a figure read aloud that is not the figure paid. The printed figure stands unchallenged over fewer bodies. He does not look into the basket. Sella’s uncalled debt against the firing of tiles stays neither paid nor settled, never done with; the soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs is still set for a measure nobody called, and the boy keeps Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on its own tray, not joined to that hand or to any other record-first hand.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; she answered the reading with the fire and said nothing about what went over the basket. Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of, and Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. Dessa has been dead more mornings than any living person keeps count of and the figure read over the basket did not know her name or the boy’s; he has never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. The soft-cuffed clerk at the Fishstairs and the man from Slate Row with soft hands are two more record-first shapes on their own trays, not Marra and not joined to one another or to the loaf. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 24 (bonds).} On Seed 22, afternoon, came up short off the north road at the outer edge of the yard well with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all; hands large and clean, wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than it required. Read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the leaning yard, said \emph{A number goes into a slate and not into a strip. If your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I} — taking himself out of his own sentence as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. A man brought a number up out of a fist toward the well, looked at it, thought better of giving it and put the fist back in his sleeve, so the figure arrived nowhere; the boy kept Berr’s twice-wiped thumb on a tray of its own beside the other record-first hands and did not join it to the neighbour’s reaching hand at the shelf or to Sella’s hand on the board. Tarn said \emph{Yes, house} to the early thaw and the late and kept wanting the late because it puts off the paying. Berr went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the narrow slate under his coat and the box locked in his house behind him and the true subtraction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with, and he never said \emph{I} or looked into the basket. Offstage on Seed 21 and 23. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 25 (bonds).} Offstage on all three days, present only as a shape in the boy’s private file: at the Fishstairs on Seed 26 the boy set Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and his finger passed over a figure beside a midwife reaching for a slate before a child, a neighbour at a well, a clerk behind a Court table, a man who priced him, Jorra speaking to the wheel before the pots, Sella giving the instruction to the wool before anyone, and Alda laying her birth-slates down before the fold — a row of record-first hands kept on separate places and never joined. At the Cross the soft-handed man from Slate Row who held his slate at the edge was filed apart from Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, with no wiped thumb, no sentence taken out of itself and no sale. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of; Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. Dessa is more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of and the figure that went nowhere in the strips did not know her name or the boy’s; he has never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 26 (bonds).} On Seed 30, Tenthday, Account-day and the last market of Seed, came up short off the north road to the reading block at the Cross, offstage on Seed 27–29. The red wool cord of his office was folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze stood at one corner of his mouth; under the hot clay was the smell of nothing at all, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands were large and clean; he wiped the thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing and held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passing a finger over the figure and letting his eyes rest on it a breath longer than the writing required. He read \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says} low into the two hundred, said \emph{The levy is called. It is not called by me}, and to a man who brought a number up out of a fist and asked what the planting cost now the hands had been in it said \emph{A number goes into a slate, not into a strip; if your house wants it again, there’ll be a slate at the watch} — \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}, taking himself out of his own sentence as a hand goes out of a field before the dressing goes on. The figure read aloud was not the figure paid, the true subtraction sat in the locked box in his house up the road, and the figure that went into the slate did not know the hand that had not come back out of the strip. He never said \emph{I} and did not look into the basket; the boy kept his twice-wiped thumb and his finger over the figure on a tray of their own, not joined to any other record-first hand. Garl’s debt against the firing of tiles went around the space where a name might have stood, neither paid nor settled nor done with, and he went off up the clay road toward High Kiln with the box locked and the true deduction inside, believing he had done the district a kindness. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 27 (bonds).} Offstage through Reed 1–3, present only as a filed shape: the twice-wiped thumb and the finger passed over a figure that was not the figure paid, kept with the other record-first hands on a tray of its own and not joined to the soft-cuffed clerk’s order of reaching, the neighbour’s hand at the shelf, the midwife’s, the wheel-keeper’s or the woman who keeps the fire. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of; Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. Dessa is more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of, the figure that arrived nowhere in the planting did not know her name or the boy’s, and the hand that did not come back out of the strip went on having no figure. He never looked into the basket and has entered this nowhere, including in his own mind. No bond was paid or repaired this chapter: the box stayed locked and the good reason intact.

\textbf{Ch 28 (bonds).} On Reed 6 he came up short off the clay road a little after midday with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, hot clay over the smell of nothing at all. Sella’s widow’s mark and Garl’s uncalled debt against the tiles were not touched or named; Jorra’s dust and the back room were not spoken of; Alda’s birth-slates and second notes stayed where they belonged. \textbf{Ch 30 (bonds).} On Reed 10, morning, the first Account-day of Reed, he came up to the reading block short, before the top of the morning, with the red wool cord of his office folded under his coat instead of worn across it and the green of tasted glaze at one corner of his mouth, the most expensive smell in Grath. His hands were large and clean; he wiped his thumb twice on his apron before touching nothing, held a narrow slate unopened against his forearm, passed a finger over the figure and let his eyes rest on the writing a breath longer than the writing required. \emph{One in twelve, as the notice says}, he read low into the goers-by; he called the levy and said \emph{The levy is called.
