\CRcharacter*{Ulda}{the friend who knew exactly what to say}{build/art/characters/ulda.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Ulda, Ulda of the Fishstairs, the foundling with the ready laugh, the boy who sold the mark}\CRfield{Role}{antagonist}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 809, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath (foundling; one name only)}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; foundling, one name only)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; no house, no kin, no slate until the Court entered him}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Fishstairs; the Waiting Room clerk; quietly, the keeping of small secrets for people who pay}\CRfield{Status}{alive — a held shape at the market’s edge on Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day of the kiln month, cast-offs catching the light on the green sliver and going dull, given no name, no dialogue, no loaf and no sale, not counted as a seventh sighting; nothing sold at the close of Day 191}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 16}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Three years older than Corin and twice as easy in the world, with a narrow face that is always slightly amused and a set of clothes that are somebody else’s cast-offs worn as if they were a uniform. He has a gap where a front tooth was knocked out at the Fishstairs and he grins through it, which makes people forgive the things he says before they have decided whether to be offended. He keeps a sliver of green lead-glaze in a string around his neck, picked up in High Kiln, and rubs it with his thumb while he decides what a person wants to hear, which is almost always the thing they have already said they want and a little more. He smells of river silt, small ale and the warm stone of other people’s hearths, because he is always in somebody’s kitchen and never in his own. The thing people notice first is the grin; the thing they notice last is that when Corin turns his head toward a pot, Ulda turns it too, a half-beat late, and has never once been able to explain why.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Fast, warm, fluent in the proverb-form of Low Kiln and quicker than the adults at it. He is the only child in the yard who can make the kiln-hands laugh, and he does it by saying the thing the adults are thinking in a voice that makes it harmless. He never says \emph{I want}; he says \emph{they say}, \emph{everyone knows}, \emph{your house wouldn’t mind}, which is a way of wanting without owning the want. When he is lying he gets affectionate, which is the tell that Mira Silt has learned to read and that Corin, for years, took for kindness. He has a habit of finishing another person’s sentence for them, correctly, and then looking surprised that it was not what they meant.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “—and a good deal,” said at the well in Ch 16, finishing a kiln-hand’s sentence in a quick, warm, affectionate voice. “That’s the whole of the account. Everyone knows it. I’m only saying.” This is his first plain sound in the book: a borrowed sentence, harmless on the surface, that makes the yard laugh before anybody has decided whether to be offended.

\item “Everyone knows the Vail boy isn’t Vail. I’m not saying it. I’m saying everyone knows it. There’s a difference.”

\item “You heard it before I tapped it, didn’t you? That’s not a trick. That’s a thing you should be careful with, Corin. I’m only saying.”

\item “I didn’t tell the clerk. I told him a thing and he wrote it down. That’s not the same, is it? You tell me, because I can never tell which part’s mine.”

\item “The mark. Under your sleeve. I saw it at the Weir and I didn’t say. I didn’t say for three years, Corin. That’s what I’m asking you to remember.”

\item “Sella’s kind to you. She’s kind to me too, when she’s thinking of something else. Don’t make it more than it is.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
He was born in Low Kiln to a mother entered in the name-pot and returned thin, and he has never known which of the several dead in him is his mother, which he describes as \emph{a family, in a manner of speaking}. He was entered on a slate at three because the Court began counting foundlings in Y.H. 782, and has had a name on a roll ever since, which makes him, in his own account, a man of property compared with Corin, who for his first years had none. He attached himself to the Vail yard at five because there was alwaysbread there and because the boy with the flower was interesting in a way Ulda could not name. He became the foundling’s friend in the way poor children become friends: by sharing a crust, by knowing which boards at the Fishstairs are safe, and by being the person who says the thing aloud that the other one is thinking.

He has sold small secrets at the Fishstairs since he was nine — which household has paid the levy, which collector takes his ale before a draw, which hearth-maid has begun to keep a second set of notes — and has never thought of it as betrayal, because a secret in Low Kiln is a thing that belongs to whoever can use it. In Y.H. 811 he told a Waiting Room clerk that a foundling under the Vail roof could hear the full note of a pot before it was tapped. The clerk wrote it down. Ulda was eleven and was paid in a loaf, and has entered the loaf in no account, which is the only thing about the whole business he has never been able to explain to himself.

Three years later he will tell the same clerk about the branching red mark under the boy’s sleeve, which he saw at the Weir and has kept for exactly the right moment, and the clerk will write that down too. He will do it because he has begun to be afraid that Corin will one day be taken by the Court and Ulda will not be there to be useful, which in his vocabulary is the same as being abandoned. He will say afterwards that he did it to protect him. He will believe it for a while.

\textbf{On his age in these chapters.} In Y.H. 813, when he first comes plainly into the yard in Chapter 16, he is a small foundling of three or four in somebody else’s cast-offs, not the eleven-year-old of the dialogue above. The sentences about the Waiting Room clerk, the paid loaf, the mark under the sleeve and the sale at eleven belong to years hence and are written here as the shape of the man he will become, not as words this child speaks now. In Chapter 16 he is given one borrowed sentence and nothing of his own; his sheet was reconciled to this on his first appearance. If he is given a second speaking appearance while the boy is still an infant, treat the later dialogue as years ahead of him and give him no secret to sell yet.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He has no house and has made a career of being the person who fits into other people’s. His wound is that he cannot want anything in his own voice: every desire comes out as \emph{they say} or \emph{everyone knows}, so that he can deny it if it is refused. He fears the name-pot, because a foundling entered on a slate can be entered again, and fears more than that the day Corin looks at him with that clinical, quiet attention and sees the thing he did at eleven. His contradiction: the boy who tells everyone’s secrets has kept one of his own for three years — the mark — and calls the keeping of it loyalty, when it is a thing he has been saving to spend.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a place in a household, any household, where the door closes on him and somebody says his name without a slate in front of them. He thinks he wants Corin to stay in Low Kiln and be his friend forever, which is the same as wanting the boy not to become what he is becoming. What he needs is to understand that a person cannot be kept by being useful, and that the loaf he was paid at eleven has gathered interest for three years in an account he cannot read. When he finally says the thing he did, it will be in the affectionate voice, and it will be the first honest sentence he has ever spoken, and Corin will not believe him at first, which is the correct response.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — his friend, the only person he has never tried to manage, which is why the betrayal will work. Ulda knows the boy hears things and has spent years pretending not to notice so that the boy will keep being ordinary beside him. The tension is a love that expresses itself as a careful inventory of the beloved’s weaknesses, held in reserve. \emph{Ch 16:} the boy in the basket is still an infant and Ulda does not know him yet; he turns his own head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy turns his, is as surprised as anybody and cannot say why, and rubs the green sliver at his neck. The half-beat is the physical tell of what he will one day do, filed in the boy’s private file without a cause written across it. \emph{Ch 18:} the delay came a second time at the market’s edge on Silt 30, half a beat after the boy’s turning and after the knuckle, and he stopped, rubbed the sliver and could not say why; no loaf, no slate, no sentence. The boy keeps the second delay on its own tray beside the first and still writes no cause across either. \emph{Ch 36:} a \textbf{sixth} silent glimpse came at the last market of Reed on Day 149 — cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in his wrists, a gap in his grin, a green sliver on a string at his throat — his head a half-beat late toward a set-down pot and stopping in the middle, the sliver rubbed twice and his mouth opening on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence with nothing a clerk could take down; no loaf passed, no slate was seen and no sale was paid, and the boy kept the shape on a place of its own, never Fenna in the narration and never named.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she reads his affection as the tell it is and has told him once, at the Fishstairs, that a boy who sells a secret has no way of buying it back. He answered with the weather and has never forgotten that she did not laugh.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he carries messages for her and has never once told her that the boy she thinks is dead is three doors away, because a secret that big would make him important, and a boy who is important gets entered on a slate.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — he is always in her kitchen and she has never once said he may not be, which he has decided is the same as being wanted and is not.

\textbf{The Waiting Room clerk} — a man whose name is not on any roll, who pays in loaves and ale and has taught Ulda that a secret is worth exactly what somebody will give for it. This is the man who will buy the mark.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — who would throw him out of the yard if he knew half of it, and whom Ulda watches carefully, because Jorra has broken three birth-slates and is therefore a person who could be useful or a person who could be dangerous.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 19 he is glimpsed once, silently, at the yard well — a small foundling in cast-off clothes worn like a uniform, a gap in his grin, the green sliver of lead-glaze at his neck. He turns his head toward a pot a half-beat after the boy’s and rubs the sliver, and is as surprised as anyone; no sentence is finished for a kiln-hand this time, no loaf passes, no slate is seen. The boy files the delay as an object on a place of its own and keeps his own turning beside it without letting the two touch. He is not seen again that week; nothing has changed hands that a slate could read and the sale stays a shape, not a betrayal paid. The half-beat and the loaf from Silt 16 gather interest in an account the child cannot read.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} He is still a shape and not a friend in the boy’s file: the Silt 16 loaf and the half-beat have gathered another seven days of interest, and nothing has crossed that any slate could read. Corin does not know him yet and he has no line of his own; Mira still reads the affection he has not learned to hide, and Sella’s kitchen door is still open without anybody saying he may not come in. Jorra would throw him out if he knew half of it, and the Waiting Room clerk still waits for a better price than a loaf. No bond changed hands on Seed 9: no loaf, no slate, no sentence finished, no secret sold.

\textbf{Ch 23 (bonds).} He is still a shape and not a friend in the boy’s file: the Silt 16 loaf and the half-beat have gathered another three days of interest and nothing has crossed that any slate could read. Corin does not know him yet and he has no line of his own; Mira still reads the affection he has not learned to hide, and Sella’s kitchen door is still open without anybody saying he may not come in. Jorra would throw him out if he knew half of it, and the Waiting Room clerk still waits for a better price than a loaf. On Seed 19 he was glimpsed once at the market’s edge, unnamed and silent, cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap in his grin and the green sliver at his throat; when a pot was set down his head went toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped, and he rubbed the sliver and opened his mouth on the tail of a kiln-hand’s sentence without finishing it. No loaf passed, no slate was seen and no secret sold; the delay stays a thing that comes after the knock, not a hearing and not a seventh, and the sale stays a shape.

\textbf{Ch 27 (bonds).} He is still a shape at the edge of the market, not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. On Reed 2 he stood at the edge of the stalls beyond the Cross in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat that caught the light when he turned and went dull when he turned back. When a kiln-hand set a pot down, his head went toward it half a beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stopped in the middle of the turn; he rubbed the sliver twice with his thumb and his mouth opened on the tail of the kiln-hand’s sentence and nothing came out that any clerk could take down. No loaf passed anywhere within reach of the basket and no slate was opened within two paces of it. This is the \textbf{fifth} glimpse, held on a place of its own beside the four earlier delays and the Silt 16 loaf, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh, and the boy wrote no cause across any of them. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk, and is joined to none of them; the sale stays a shape and the betrayal stays years ahead.

\textbf{Ch 46 (bonds).} On Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, he was a held shape at the market’s edge, unnamed in the narration and given no dialogue: cast-offs catching the light on the green sliver at his throat and going dull when he turned, no pot set down for him to turn toward, no half-beat spent, no loaf passed, no slate opened within reach of the basket and no sale paid. The boy gave the colour no ear and the shape no name, and did not count him as a seventh sighting (T033/T034 held; the no-seventh-in-Chapters-46–50 rule kept). He is not the man carried out on Day 188 and not the green at the pot board’s mouth; the sixth green stays a colour and this stays a shape, on places of their own and not joined. He is not Marra, not the Fishstairs clerk and not the Court-table clerk, and is joined to none of them. The Silt 16 loaf goes on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and any dialogue on his sheet remains years ahead of the child in the basket. No bond changed hands, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
He enters in Chapter 16 as the grin at the well, finishing a kiln-hand’s sentence in the affectionate voice that makes the yard laugh, a small foundling of three or four in a coat with a man’s shoulders and breeches cut off at the knee, worn like a uniform he was never measured for. The gap where a front tooth had been goes into every circle of the yard ahead of him and comes back with permission to say anything; the sliver of green lead-glaze on a string at his neck is rubbed with his thumb while he decides what a person wants to hear, which is usually what the person has already said and a little more. He says what everybody is thinking in a tone that makes it harmless, and he never says \emph{I want} --- he says \emph{they say}, \emph{everyone knows}, \emph{your house wouldn’t mind}. When a woman sets a pot down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops and comes back; he rubs the green sliver and cannot say why he turned, and is as surprised as anybody. When a man from Slate Row whose name is on no roll holds out a warm loaf, his mouth opens on a sentence with the shape of \emph{everyone} or \emph{your house} and stops where a want would have stood, because he has no form of words for a want that is his own and is too quick a child to say a thing that could be refused to him by name. The loaf goes into the pocket of the cast-off coat, which holds a bit of string and nothing any clerk could read, with no slate between them; the man says something low that does not carry and the child nods as though he had understood it. He is named on the sheet but not in the narration. He stays a shape in the boy’s file --- a delay, a sliver, a loaf, an unfinished sentence --- and no secret has changed hands that any slate could read, no betrayal has been paid. The loaf has begun to gather interest in an account he cannot read, and the half-beat is held for the day it lands as the physical tell of what he did.

On Days 78 through 84 he is a shape at the edge of the recovery, not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He appears once, at the yard well on Silt 19, in cast-offs worn like a uniform with a green sliver at his throat; when a pot is set down his head goes toward it a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, and he stops, rubs the sliver and cannot say why he turned. The boy files the delay beside his own turning without letting the two touch, because a thing that comes after the knock is a different thing from one that comes before it and this was neither a hearing nor a seventh. No acceleration of a kiln-hand’s sentence, no warm loaf, no slate, no secret; he is gone for the rest of the week and nothing has been sold that any clerk could read. The half-beat stays the physical tell held for the day the small sales land as betrayal, and the loaf from the man from Slate Row goes on gathering interest in an account he cannot read.

On Days 107 through 109 he is a shape at the edge of the planting month’s last tend, still not a speaker and not yet a betrayer. He is glimpsed once on Seed 19 at the dawn market below the north bridge, unnamed in the narration, at the edge of the fish-trade shade where a whole market walks carefully over the out-of-line landing and a soft-cuffed clerk sits for a measure nobody called. He is in cast-offs worn like a uniform, silt dried pale in the creases of his wrists, a gap where a front tooth had been and a green sliver of lead-glaze on a string at his throat. When a kiln-hand sets a pot down near the eel shade the boy hears its full note and his head goes toward it; the foundling’s head goes a half-beat after the boy’s, after the knuckle and after the note, then stops in the middle of the turn. He rubs the sliver twice with his thumb and could not have said why he turned, and there is no word in the market’s language for the thing that made him turn, which was not the note and came after it. A kiln-hand at the edge says the tail of a sentence and leaves it hanging, and the foundling’s mouth opens on the end of it the way a child’s mouth opens to finish a thing heard a hundred times, and nothing comes out that any clerk could have taken down. No loaf passes, no slate is opened within reach of the basket and no secret changes hands that a slate could read. Somewhere a long way off a hand will lay them together and call the joining an account; it is not his hand and it is not today. On Ember 10, the first Account-day of the kiln month, he is a shape at the market’s edge again: cast-offs, a gap in his grin, the green sliver at his throat catching the light and going dull. He is given no name, no dialogue, no half-beat, no loaf and no sale, and the boy does not count him as a seventh sighting. The rule for these chapters holds him to a shape on a place of his own, after the knock and not before it, not a hearing and not a seventh; the sixth green at the pot board stays a colour and is not joined to the sliver. He is not Marra, not the clerk at the Fishstairs and not the clerk at the Court’s table, and is joined to none of them. The Silt 16 loaf goes on gathering interest in an account the child cannot read, and the betrayal stays years ahead.

\CRcharacter{Hessa Rale}{the woman who carries the figure and never reads it}{build/portraits/hessa-rale.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Hessa, Hessa of Slate Row, the runner, the slate-runner}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{unknown; a woman of Slate Row, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{Slate Row, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Allegiance}{carries slates between the Cross at Sill and Greybank for the Thane of Clay; no house of her own spoken of}\CRfield{Status}{alive — seen on Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, going up the clay road to Greybank before noon with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned to her sleeve; to two women who asked what she carried said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, answering the question put and not the one behind it; her figure still unread, carried and not joined to any keeping}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 38}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
A woman of thirty-odd years with the drained, level face of somebody who has walked the same road too often to measure it any more. Nothing about her is arranged for looking at: her coat is shortened at the skirt for the road’s mud, and the mud has dried on it in a pale scurf which she does not brush off, because a runner’s coat is a tool and nobody scours a tool for its own sake. A strap crosses her chest and a second, shorter strap has been let out to take the weight when the road is long; she settles both without seeming to, the way a person settles a burden that has become part of the walk. Her hands are the hands of a woman who carries and does not open. The fingers close on a slate’s edge with a working looseness, the thumb lies along the grain of the frame, and nothing presses where the writing is. She holds the slate edge-on to her own forearm so that the face of it turns toward her sleeve and the writing looks at nobody. That is not concealment: it is the manner of carrying a slate so the writing is not rubbed and no goer-by takes a figure off it without a hand to put there. She moves at the pace of a person who has made a bargain with distance and keeps it without thinking. What people notice first is the slate; what they notice last, if they notice at all, is that her hand went to it before her eyes went to them.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Clipped, practical, the grammar of the road rather than the Court. She answers the question actually put and not the one behind it, and she is done with a conversation when the road is done with it, without rudeness and without apology. She never pronounces, never reads aloud, never says \emph{the account} or \emph{the figure} where \emph{the slate} will do. Her sentences are short and complete; what she will not carry she leaves standing where it was set down, the way a man leaves a pot where there is no hand to carry it. A slight dry amusement goes with the road and not with people.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which.”

\item “Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk.”

\item “Ask the road. It knows the way and I know the weight. That’s the whole of what either of us knows.”

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She comes out of Slate Row, where the Court’s tables and the Waiting Room stand and where a person can be made answerable for a thing merely by having touched it. She took up running because it was work that could be measured in the legs and kept in the hands: a slate goes from the Cross to Greybank and back, and what is written on it belongs to the person who set it down. Over the years she has carried slates for the assessor’s house, for the collector’s table at the Cross, and for Berr Clay the Thane, whose narrow slate goes up the clay road ahead of the reading and comes back with the true subtraction nobody in Sill has been shown. She has never been asked to read one and has never offered. The district is full of people who put a hand to a record before they put an eye to a person; she is one of them and does not know it, or does not think about it, which amounts to the same thing from the outside. She knows the road in all weathers, knows which ruts hold water and which stretch of the clay road dries pale in scurf, and has made a bargain with distance that she keeps without thinking. Nothing in her history has yet made her a reader of anyone’s private keeping, and she is careful that nothing does.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
No wound is spoken of. Her hands carry the small wear of a working person who grips an edge and not a face: nails short, thumb callused along one side from the frame of a slate, the skin at the wrist hardened by a strap. She fears a slate rubbed blank in a coat, a strap parting on the road, and being made answerable for a figure she did not set down; these are the fears of a carrier, not of a clerk. She has seen what happens to a person in Slate Row who is caught between a figure and the person it is about, and she keeps her own face turned toward the sleeve.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants the road kept, the slates delivered whole, and to be paid for carrying and never for knowing. She thinks she wants nobody to take an interest in what she carries. What she needs, years from now, is harder: to understand that a figure is not a thing that travels by itself, and that the hand which lays the district’s separate keepings together will one day be a hand like hers — a carrier’s hand that has learned, too late, what it has been carrying. That day is far off and she is not yet part of it.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — she carries his narrow slate between the Cross and Greybank and does not read it. He is a good reason in a neat hand; she is the road under it. On Day 158 his cord was spoken of as a direction up the clay road, and on Day 159 she took the slate up that road ahead of the reading, after he had called the levy and denied it with \emph{your house}, never \emph{I}. No loyalty is spoken and no figure passes between them.

\textbf{The Cross and Greybank} — the two ends of her road. At the Cross the reading goes up before noon; at Greybank the factor and the bank are. She joins the two places without ever joining what is written at either.

\textbf{Sella Vail and the Vail basket} — on Day 158 she came through the Clay Yard and Sella carried the boy past at the half-pace, gave the house no name for the slate and did not say whose it was. Neither woman asked the other anything. At the Cross on Day 159 Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay.

\textbf{The boy under the Vail roof} — he does not know her name and she has not looked into the basket. He saw the order of her reaching and filed it as the eighth record-first hand in the district, on a place of its own, joined to none. She has no idea she has been filed.

\textbf{Ch 40 (bonds).} On the second Account-day of Tallow she is seen again going up the clay road with Berr’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm, her hand to it before her eyes go to the crowd, the small flat correction of the strap and the turn of the wrist bringing the edge round; her coat is shortened at the skirt for the road’s mud with the dried pale scurf unbrushed, two straps settled, thumb along the grain of the frame and nothing pressing where the writing is. To a woman who asks what she carries: \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which}; to the woman who wants more: \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk.} No figure comes off the slate and no joining is made to Marra, the clerks, the reed-cutter’s cord, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the finger beneath the loaf shelf or the soft-cuffed clerk at the landing. She is a runner and not a reader; the order of her reaching remains the eighth record-first hand on a place of its own (T080 advanced, not paid).

\textbf{Ch 42 (bonds).} On the third Account-day of Tallow she went up the clay road to Greybank before noon with Berr’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm, the writing turned to her sleeve and her hand arriving before her eyes. To a woman who asked what she carried she said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference}; to the next question, \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, answering the question put and not the one behind it. No figure came off the slate. She was not joined to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate, Marra, the other record-first hands or any keeping; what she carries stays a thing somebody else set down. No bond paid, no new scar or possession, no change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 46 (bonds).} On Day 189, Ember 10, the first Account-day and market-day of the kiln month, she went up the clay road to Greybank before noon with Berr Clay’s narrow slate edge-on to her forearm and the writing turned to her sleeve, her hand to the slate before her eyes to the crowd; the second strap was let out for the long road and the dried pale scurf of the mud stood unbrushed on the shortened skirt. To two women who asked what she carried she said \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}, answering the question put and not the one behind it. No figure came off the slate. She was not joined to Berr’s twice-wiped thumb, the soft-cuffed clerk’s inward slate at the out-of-line landing, Marra, the other record-first hands or any keeping; her order of reaching stayed the eighth such hand on a place of its own, advanced and not paid (T080). Sella set the basket in the moot-post’s finger’s width of shade where no slate lay and stood half a pace off, gave the runner no name and asked nothing about the slate. No bond paid, no new scar or possession, no change of voice; she is a runner and not a reader.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
She enters in the firing month of Y.H. 813, on the eve of the first Account-day of Tallow, and is seen twice: once coming through the Clay Yard from the direction of the Cross with Berr Clay’s narrow slate held edge-on to her forearm, and once the next morning taking it up the clay road toward Greybank. In the yard a woman asked what the levy would take now the kilns had been brought up and hands were in the month; Hessa answered that she did not read it, she carried it, that there was a difference and the road did not care which; when the woman wanted more she said \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk} and went on through the yard, leaving the question standing where it had been set down. Her hand went to the slate before her eyes went to the people, the small flat correction of the strap and a turn of the wrist to bring the edge round. To the boy that order of reaching is an eighth such hand-shape in the district, kept on its own place beside Marra’s pause, the neat dark hand, the Court-table clerk, the soft-cuffed clerk at the landing, the soft hands at Slate Row, Berr’s twice-wiped thumb and the finger that goes beneath the Vail loaf shelf. He does not let eight likenesses trouble him into a rule, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them. At the Cross on the Account-day she came through again with the slate edge-on, hand to slate before eye to the crowd, and went up the clay road with the writing turned to her sleeve; no figure came off it under any roof in Sill. She is a runner and not a reader of anyone’s private keeping, and the figure on the slate remained what figures on carried slates remained in this district: a thing somebody else had set down and nobody here had read.

She enters the second Account-day of the firing month as she entered the first: a figure going up the road in a narrow slate held edge-on, the writing turned toward a sleeve and the hand arriving before the eyes. The road between Cross and Greybank is the whole of her account, and she joins the two ends without joining what is written at either. The district is full of hands that put a record before a person; hers is one more such hand and she has made a manner of it, so that a slate is carried and no figure is read and nothing in it becomes hers to answer for. The boy has filed the order once and does not file it twice; eight likenesses must still be held apart by hand, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them.

She enters the third Account-day of the firing month as she entered the first: a figure going up the clay road in a narrow slate held edge-on, the writing turned toward a sleeve and the hand arriving before the eyes. The road between Cross and Greybank is the whole of her account, and she joins the two ends without joining what is written at either. To a woman who asks what she carries she answers the question put and not the one behind it, and goes on with the road’s pace. The boy has filed her order of reaching once and does not file it twice; eight likenesses must still be held apart by hand, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them. She is still a runner and not a reader of anyone’s private keeping.

She enters the first Account-day of the kiln month as she entered those of the firing month: a figure going up the clay road in a narrow slate held edge-on, the writing turned toward a sleeve and the hand arriving before the eyes. On Day 189 she takes Berr’s slate up the road toward Greybank before noon, the second strap let out for the long road and the mud dried in pale scurf on the shortened skirt, and answers the question put and not the one behind it with \emph{I don’t read it. I carry it. There’s a difference, and the road doesn’t care which} and \emph{Cross to Greybank. Reading goes up before noon. I’ve got a road to walk}. No figure comes off the slate. The boy has filed her order of reaching once and does not file it twice; eight likenesses must still be held apart by hand, for a rule wants a payer and no payer has been named to any of them. She is still a runner and not a reader of anyone’s private keeping.

\CRcharacter*{Tarn Vail}{the debt with hands}{build/art/characters/tarn.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Tarn, the Vail’s Tarn, Tarn of the Yard}\CRfield{Role}{other}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 790, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic; returned thin)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; no house of his own}\CRfield{Allegiance}{House Vail, clay-bound for seven years from Y.H. 806}\CRfield{Status}{alive — clay-bound, with the seventh year nearer its end than it has ever stood and still held, the breath from Seed 16 still unspent, nine stoppings still nine objects with no tenth stood up and the loan still uncalled at the close of Day 185, Ember 6; through Ember 4–6 he took the broom only after it had been instructed, told the kindling \emph{Six counted. The next I don’t count}, six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh held at the lip where it cannot, with Garl’s unforged sentence beside the knife, the ear-sentence short of the word that would call the loan on all three days; he wanted the late thaw because it puts off the paying, swept the collector’s road without turning and no collector came; his stroke went over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check, so the Day 171 movement stayed a held change on its own place beside the Day 161 damper fraction and the Day 166 shelf beat; Ash worked into the knuckle creases in the colour of the clean dark line, pale clip-ring at the left wrist; \textbf{the chapter’s one meaningful change:} on the afternoon of Day 183 he took the warm stone Sella gave him in the winter Garl died out of its unmarked clay pot in the Debt Loft, two years gone and cold and not looked at in a year, held it, set it on the sill where the finger’s-width opening let in light, looked at it a long moment and put it back — no word, no figure, no payer, no slate, not reconciled and not forgiven, for not trying is not forgiving; the stone lies back in the pot, cold, and the debt stands as it stood (T006 advanced, T036/T076 advanced, not paid); through Days 186–188, Ember 7–9, the seventh year stands nearer its end than it has ever stood and is still held, six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh held at the lip where it cannot, the Seed 16 breath unspent with its small interval, nine stoppings still nine objects with no tenth before the seventh year is earned, the ear-sentence brought to the threshold of the word that calls the loan on all three days and stopped there with no figure and no name, the loan uncalled, his stroke over the flagstones past the shallow bright patch without the half-check; the warm stone lies back in its pot in the loft, cold and unreconciled, and the remembering is filed as a remembering and not a holding made again; through Days 189–191, Ember 10–12, the seventh year stands nearer its end than it has ever stood and is still held, six counted in the worn thumb-mark where the house can check and the seventh at the lip where it cannot, the knife at the edge of its sill with Garl’s unforged collector sentence beside it, the Seed 16 breath unspent, nine stoppings still nine objects with no tenth, the ear-sentence short of the word that would call the loan on all three days, the loan uncalled, his stroke over the flagstones past the bright patch without the half-check, Ash worked into the knuckle creases and the pale clip-ring at the left wrist; the stone lies cold and unreconciled in its pot in the loft}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 2}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Twenty-two and bent at the shoulders from six years in the slip pit, which makes him look older than his term. He has grey Ash in the creases of his knuckles that no amount of scrubbing lifts, and a pale ring round his left wrist where an iron clip sat in Y.H. 806, when he was bound. He is a narrow man with a narrow face and the habit of putting the smallest tool on the bench into his pocket when he thinks nobody is looking, because a man who owns nothing should know where the small things are. He sleeps in the Debt Loft above the wheel-shed and keeps his few possessions in a clay pot with no mark on it. He smells of wet wool, tallow and the sour tang of a corner that has not been swept. The thing people notice first is how quickly he moves; the thing they notice last is that he stops moving altogether when he is told he is doing well.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Deferential with a nail in it. He calls everyone \emph{house}, including Sella, and says \emph{I owe} where another man would say \emph{I am}. He never argues; he agrees so thoroughly that the argument has nowhere to go. When he is frightened he becomes helpful, which in a kiln-house means doing three things at once and quietly putting the fourth right. His jokes are not jokes; they are statements of fact made in a tone that invites someone else to laugh so that he does not have to.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Yes, house. I’ll sweep it. I swept it this morning. I’ll sweep it again.”

\item “Six years. One to go. I’ve counted every one, and I won’t count the next.”

\item “He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.”

\item “You can’t return a man to himself. They tried with my mother. She came back with somebody else’s hands.”

\item “I took the small knife. I put it back. You can check.” --- said of his own accord, to nobody, in the tone of a man stating the weather.

\item “Six counted. The next I don’t count.” --- to the kindling at the going of the light, with the knife set back where it can be checked; the sentence about the ear under this roof came a sixth time on Reed 20 to the word that would call the loan and stopped there with no figure and no name, the breath drawn and not spent.

\item “Yes, house.” --- said on Day 140 to an early thaw and a late, wanting the late because it puts off the paying, though the paying has stood in the ruts since the water went.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
His mother was banked in Y.H. 792 and came back thin to the district’s name-pot, with fragments of a life she could not name and hands that frightened him because they were not her hands. He was born of that return, which means he carries a little of somebody else’s interest in a life he cannot place, and has been told all his life that this makes him useful. In Y.H. 806, at sixteen, his mother’s account was entered against him and he was bound to House Vail for seven years, a term he did not choose and has counted every day of. He has worked the slip pits, swept the yard, banked the fire and carried the household’s small accounts in his head for six years.

He was sent to fetch a collector for Garl Vail in the Long Cold and turned back at the frozen ford. Sella never asked whether he had gone. Jorra, who was thirteen, never asked either, which Tarn has decided is worse. He was in the house when Corin arrived and watched the boy be given a bed while he slept in the loft, and he has never said the thing he thinks about it, because a clay-bound hand who complains about beds is a clay-bound hand who can be returned to the slate.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
He is a debt with a body, and one year of a seven-year term left. He fears that when the term ends there will be no house to take him and he will be entered again for vagrancy, which is how the district keeps people. He fears the Second Want in himself — the shape that comes over him some nights and leaves him reaching for a tool he has never used. He fears Sella’s kindness more than Jorra’s command, because the kindness is the thing he cannot enter in any account and therefore cannot pay back. His contradiction: the man who owns nothing is the one who notices when a tool is missing and the one who keeps the house’s accounts most exactly.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
He wants a slate with his own name on it and no mark against it. He wants to be called by something that is not a house’s possession. He thinks he wants freedom; what he needs is to learn that freedom in Sarn is another category of account, and that a man can be unowned and still be cold, and that the thing to want is not an empty column but a way to keep warm without being spent.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Sella Vail} — she holds his debt and once, in the winter Garl died, gave him a warm stone for the loft which he has kept in his clay pot for two years. He cannot reconcile the stone with the debt, and has stopped trying, which is not the same as forgiving it. \emph{Ch 2:} he calls her \emph{house}, says \emph{I owe} where another man says \emph{I am}, and agreed with everything so thoroughly that there was nowhere for an argument to go. She gave the foundling a bed and him the loft, and he put the one sentence into the room that nobody had asked for.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — son of the house, who treats him as a brother when the wheel needs him and as a servant when it does not. Tarn has decided to hate him for it and keeps failing, because Jorra once sat up all night with him through a fever and has never mentioned it. \emph{Ch 2:} Jorra noticed a rasp left out of its place and Tarn answered him; the kindness and the command arrived in the same voice and Tarn did not separate them.

\textbf{Corin} — the foundling who arrived and was given a bed in the house. Tarn was the first to notice that the boy turns his head toward a pot before anyone taps it, and has told nobody, because a clay-bound hand who can hear the full note is worth more than his debt and he does not want to be bought. \emph{Ch 2:} he said \emph{He’s a foundling. I’m a debt. Don’t put us in the same sentence, Sella.} His resentment is not envy of the bed; it is a man keeping the one thing he owns, which is the exact account of what he is owed and what he owes.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — he has carried messages between her and the house, and barley from her to Sella, and has hated being the thin part of that chain. He knows her cough is not the pits and has never said so.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — she has suspected for a year that he is more than he says, and has not asked. He has noticed her noticing, and has answered her with the weather every time.

\textbf{Garl Vail} — he was sent for a collector and turned back. The dead man’s coat still hangs behind the door and Tarn has never once touched it.

\textbf{Ch 4.} He called Sella \emph{house} and put the knife back twice where it could be checked; his broom stopped two strokes at the Vail pot’s note without a turn of the head, and the boy watched and kept the silence as carefully as he did. Six of seven years counted, the seventh not. Jorra came in from the back room with slate dust and said the back room was cold; Tarn said nothing about that either. Dessa’s cough went by him as weather, as it always did. The one thing he owns stays kept.

\textbf{Ch 5.} On Stone 13 he came up the yard with the knife already back on its sill, went through the motion of checking it with his eyes, and saw the boy turn his head toward a pot \emph{before} it was set down. His broom stopped half a stroke at the soft set-down that gave nothing, and he said nothing about either thing, as he has said nothing about the pot’s note through the wall. He counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back; when Sella told him he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths, then began again. At dusk he set the knife back where it could be checked and told the yard he had done so, unasked. He wants his exact account and grudges the house the loan of a bed; a loan that can hear is a loan that can be called, and he has said neither sentence.

\textbf{Ch 6.} On Stone 16 he measured the kindling stack with his eyes --- four, four, a space where the fifth should be --- and told the stack six were counted and the seventh held back. On Stone 17 the knife went back on the sill and was announced to the empty yard, and when Sella said \emph{you’ve done well} the broom stopped altogether for two breaths before he said \emph{Yes, house} and went on; he scraped Ash from his knuckles, held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist up to the light, and put the knife back, this time without announcing it. He named the kiln’s breath as the thing that takes a man in his sleep and told of the man in Mud End the district called merciful; he wanted the late thaw because it put off the paying. His broom stopped half a stroke at the bench where no note came. On Stone 20 he told the yard again that the knife was back where it could be checked; six of seven years counted, the seventh held back, and he offered to check the ridge. He said nothing about the boy’s ear and the boy said nothing about his.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 22 his head turned a degree when a vessel carried past the door gave its flat note, and he went back to the broom without looking at the basket or calling the sound a sound; he had been sent for the collector who came with grey fingertips, and the boy put that grey on a tray of its own. On Stone 25 his broom checked half a stroke at the place in the yard where a pot cracked all the way through, and again at the place on the bench where no note had come, and he said nothing about either. He set the small knife on its sill and told the empty yard where it was on Stone 22, Stone 23 and Stone 30; counted six years of the seven and held the seventh back every day; held the pale clip-ring at his left wrist to the light; and wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Stone 29 he offered to check the width of the ridge with his thumb and took his eyes off it as a man takes his eyes off a woman who has been crying. The two silences under one roof kept their usual shape, and the loan that could hear went on being worth more than the debt that held him.

\textbf{Ch 8.} Through the Five the knife went back to its sill and the seventh year was held back every day; he announced the knife to the empty yard and said to the kindling that six were counted and the next he did not count. The Ash in the creases of his knuckles was the colour of the ridge no scrubbing lifted, and he kept the silence about the flat note all five days, as he kept the silence about the boy’s ear. On the Long Night he said in the dark that six years were counted and the next he did not, and set the knife where it could be checked; Garl’s coat held a broader man’s shape in the dark and he let the proverb go to the pot. He wanted the late thaw still, because a late thaw puts off the paying, and on Ilmen 1 he swept toward the thaw and the slip pits with the knife on its sill and the seventh year held back again.

\textbf{Ch 9.} Through Days 31–37 the knife went back to its sill and he announced it to the empty yard, six years counted and the seventh held back, Ash worked into the knuckles that no scrubbing lifted. He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, and kept wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. On Ilmen 6 his head went a degree toward the pot that answered nearly full and he went back to his broom without naming the sound or looking at the basket; the boy kept the turning beside his own hearing and did not join them. On Ilmen 7 he was with the yard at the well when the Singing Sill gave its note early and did not say what it was. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled and the sentence was not said under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 10.} The small knife goes back to its sill before light and is announced to the empty yard --- \emph{It’s back. You can check} --- with six years of the seven counted and the seventh held where he always holds it; Ash is worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring catches what light there is. He sweeps around the place where the clay-heavy water came up behind the racks and sweeps the road down toward the Fishstairs over and over without once looking along it, which is the road a man goes down when a house wants a collector. No collector comes for the woman in the brook and he does not go for one, and he does not say the omission has a name. He still wants the thaw late because a late thaw puts off the paying; he agrees with the early and the late without taking either side. The loan that can hear is still uncalled and the sentence is still unsaid under the roof.

\textbf{Ch 11.} The small knife went back to its sill before the light was gone on Days 45 and 46 and he told the empty yard where it was, unasked; on Day 47 he put it back and told nobody, because the yard had already been told and a man does not say the same thing twice to a house that does not answer. Six years of the seven were counted and the seventh held back on all three mornings, the one entry in this house the house cannot check. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning to look along it, and no collector went down it for the woman the brook took nine mornings ago; he did not say the thing which had not happened had a name. Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles that no scrubbing lifts and the pale clip-ring caught the light. He agreed with the ones who wanted the thaw early and the ones who wanted it late and kept wanting the late one, because a late thaw puts off the paying. When Sella said he had done well he stopped altogether for two breaths before saying \emph{Yes, house}.

\textbf{Ch 12.} He kept Sella’s house in its exact account and kept his own seventh year out of it; he said house to the yard and counted six where the house could check and the seventh where it could not. With the boy he kept the older equality: a vessel gave its note past the door on Day 50 and a pot answered nearly full on Day 52, and his head did not turn at either and he said nothing about either. Jorra’s returned dust went unremarked and Mira passed without a question. The loan that can hear stayed uncalled, and he still wanted the late thaw because a late thaw puts off the paying.

\textbf{Ch 13.} He agreed with the neighbour who wanted the thaw early and the one who wanted it late, saying \emph{Yes, house} to both, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying. The small knife was back on its sill with six years counted and the seventh held back, the one entry in this house the house cannot check; Ash was worked into the creases of his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the light and gave it back. His broom went over the road a man takes when a house wants a collector, over and over, without once turning along it, and no collector went down it for the woman in the brook. A vessel gave its note past the yard door on Ilmen 28 and his head did not turn; he did not name the sound or supply a Grathic word for it, and the boy did not call it a seventh hearing. Sella told him he had done well and he stopped altogether for two breaths, then set the knife where it could be checked and went back to the broom.

\textbf{Ch 14.} Before light on Silt 3 the small knife went back to its sill and was announced to the empty yard — \emph{It’s back. You can check} — and he told the kindling six were counted and the next he did not count; six years stood, and the seventh was nearly gone and still held, the one entry in this house the house could not check. Ash was worked into his knuckles in the colour of the clean dark line, and the pale clip-ring at his left wrist held the little light and gave it back. He said \emph{Yes, house} to the ones who wanted the thaw early and to the ones who wanted it late, agreed so entirely that no argument could find a foot, and went on wanting the late one because a late thaw puts off the paying, though the water came with the paying. His broom checked half a stroke at the place where a pot cracked on Stone 25 and went on without a turn of the head or a name for the sound. When a vessel gave its note past the yard door he did not turn. On Silt 6 his head went a degree toward a pot that answered nearly full under nobody’s knuckle, and then went back to the broom; he said nothing and did not look toward the basket. The boy kept his turning beside his own hearing and did not join them, and the loan that can hear stayed uncalled.
